en: Mahāniddesa:
Exposition of the Sāriputta-sutta, Chapter 16 of the Aṭṭhakavagga.
Now he will explain the exposition of the Sāriputta-sutta:
"Never before have I seen [this],
O Venerable Sāriputta," and so forth.
Nor has it been heard by anyone else:
thus the Teacher, so sweet in his discourse,
has come from the Tusita realm to lead the assembly.
"I have not seen him before this.
Previously, with these eyes and in this physical form, that Blessed One had never been seen by me.

When the Blessed One, having completed the rains retreat at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree on the yellow sandalwood stone slab in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, surrounded by a host of deities, descended to the city of Saṅkassa by means of a staircase made of jewels—this sight had not been seen by me before.
"I have not seen [such a one] before this," said the Venerable Sāriputta.
"Iccā" (thus) refers to the connection of words, the junction of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequential order of words.
"Thus it is.
"Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment, a term of respect; it is a term expressing reverence and deference—this is what "venerable" means.
"Sāriputta" is the name, designation, description, convention, appellation, naming, denomination, expression, phrasing, and utterance of that elder;
thus he is called "Venerable Sāriputta.
"Nor was it heard from anyone"—this refers to the source of his knowledge.
This is not a negation.
"Udā" is the conjunction of words, the meeting of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequential order of words— this is "udā."
“Of anyone” means: of a khattiya, or a brahmin, or a vessa, or a sudra, or a householder, or one gone forth, or a deva, or a human—has it not been heard by anyone?
Thus the Teacher speaks with charming words.
Thus his speech was elegant, sweet, endearing, heart-stirring, and possessed a voice as lovely as the song of the karavīka bird.
Furthermore, the voice issuing from the mouth of that Blessed One was endowed with eight qualities:
it was distinct, intelligible, melodious, worth hearing, clear, far-reaching, deep, and resonant.

Furthermore, in whatever assembly that Blessed One makes himself understood by his voice, no sound issues forth outside that assembly; for that Blessed One has a Brahma-voice, speaking like a karavīka bird—thus he is one whose speech is charming.
"Teacher" means the Blessed One is the Teacher, the Caravan-Leader.
Just as a caravan leader leads beings across the wilderness— across the wilderness of robbers, the wilderness of wild beasts, the wilderness of famine,
and the wilderness of waterlessness— leading them out, bringing them through, carrying them across, and establishing them in a land of safety;
even so does the Blessed One, the caravan leader, lead beings across the wilderness— across the wilderness of birth, the wilderness of old age...
He carries them across; he carries them across the wilderness of disease …pe… the wilderness of death … the wilderness of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

He carries them across the wilderness of lust, the wilderness of hatred, the wilderness of delusion, the wilderness of conceit, the wilderness of views, the wilderness of the defilements, and the wilderness of misconduct.
He carries them across the thicket of lust, the thicket of hatred, and the thicket of delusion.
… He carries across, brings out, leads forth, and delivers others from the thicket of conceit, the thicket of views, the thicket of defilements, and the thicket of misconduct;
he causes them to reach the security, the deathless, Nibbāna.
In this way too, the Blessed One is the Caravan Leader.

Alternatively, the Blessed One is the leader, the trainer, the one who guides, the one who makes known, the one who inspires reflection, the one who causes to see, and the one who inspires confidence.
In this way too, the Blessed One is the Caravan Leader.
Alternatively, the Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, and the declarer of the undeclared path.

"He is the proclaimer of the path, the knower of the path, the one who understands the path, the one skilled in the path; and his disciples now dwell following the path, having subsequently attained it.
In this way too, the Blessed One is the Caravan Leader.
"Thus the Teacher spoke so charmingly:
'The Tusita host has arrived.
This means that the Blessed One, having passed away from the Tusita realm, entered his mother's womb mindful and clearly comprehending.
In this way, he has come from the assembly of the Tusita [heaven].
Alternatively, the gods are called Tusita;
they are joyful, well-contented, elated, glad, and filled with rapture and happiness, having come from the world of the gods to the assembly.
In this way, the Tusitas have come to the assembly.
Alternatively, "Tusitas" refers to the Arahants;
they are called Tusitas because they are joyful, well-contented, glad at heart, and their aspirations are fulfilled—thus, the assembly of Arahants has arrived.
Thus also, he came from the Tusita realm as the Leader of the Assembly (*gaṇin*).
"Leader of the Assembly" means the Blessed One is a leader;

he is a leader because he is the teacher of the assembly, a leader because he is the instructor of the assembly, a leader because he sustains the assembly, and a leader because he exhorts the assembly.
A leader (*gaṇī*): one is a leader because they instruct a group; one is a leader because they approach a group with confidence;

one is a leader because they desire to hear from the group, lend an ear, and apply their mind to understanding; one is a leader because they cause the group to emerge from unwholesome states and establish them in the wholesome;
a leader of a group of monks, a leader of a group of nuns, a leader of a group of laymen, and a leader of a group of laywomen.

He is a leader, a leader of the royal assembly, a leader of the kṣatriya assembly, a leader of the brahmin assembly, a leader of the vaiśya assembly, a leader of the śūdra assembly, a leader of the assembly of gods, and a leader of the assembly of Brahmās; he is one who has a following, a leader, and a teacher of assemblies.
He has arrived, approached, drawn near, and reached the city of Saṅkassa.
The Tusita host has arrived.
Therefore, the Elder Sāriputta said:
"Never before have I seen..."
(Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Nor have I heard it from anyone else:
that the Teacher is so sweetly eloquent."
“From Tuṣita he has come to the assembly,” so it is seen by the One with Vision throughout the world including its devas.

Having dispelled all darkness, he alone attained delight in the world with its devas, its Māras, and its Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. "In the world with its devas" means: in the world with its devas, its Māras, and its Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
Of the world with its devas.

"As one who possesses eyes sees" means that just as the devas see the Blessed One seated upon the yellow sandalwood stone at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven teaching the Dhamma, so too do humans see him;
and just as humans see him, so too do the devas see him.
Just as it appears to the gods, so it appears to humans;
just as it appears to humans, so it appears to the gods.
Thus too does it appear to one who possesses vision.

Or just as some venerable recluses and brahmins who are undisciplined appear with the appearance of being disciplined, who are not peaceful appear with the appearance of being peaceful, who are not calmed appear with the appearance of being calmed, and who are not extinguished appear with the appearance of being extinguished—
like a counterfeit clay earring,
or like a half-penny of base metal covered in gold.
“They wander in the world concealed by their retinue,
impure within but appearing beautiful without.
But the Blessed One is not seen in such a way.
The Blessed One, by means of that which is real, true, such, according to reality, non-perverted, and of its own nature, appears with the appearance of one who is tamed;
he appears with the appearance of one who is calm; he appears with the appearance of one who is thoroughly pacified; he appears with the appearance of one who has attained extinction;
and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, possess unassumed postures and are endowed with their original vows.
Thus it is seen by one who possesses vision.
Alternatively, the Blessed One— whose name is pure, whose fame has spread, and whose reputation is renowned— is present in the abode of the nāgas, the abode of the supaṇṇas,
the abode of the yakkhas, the abode of the asuras, the abode of the gandhabbas, the abode of the great kings, and the abode of Indra.
"In the abode of Brahmā and in the abode of the gods, such as this and like that, and even more than that"—
thus it is seen by one who possesses vision. Alternatively,
the Blessed One is endowed with the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the four analytical knowledges.
By means of the six direct knowledges, the six qualities of a Buddha, and by means of his splendor, power, virtue, energy, and wisdom,
he is seen, known, and made manifest.
"The virtuous shine even from afar."
Like the Himavat mountain,
those who are non-existent are not seen here,
like arrows shot in the night.
And so it is as one with vision sees.
"One with vision," the Blessed One said, is one who possesses vision by means of five kinds of vision:

he is one with vision by means of the fleshly eye, he is one with vision by means of the divine eye, he is one with vision by means of the wisdom-eye, he is one with vision by means of the Buddha-eye, and he is one with vision by means of the universal eye.
In what way is the Blessed One possessed of vision even by means of the fleshly eye?
In the Blessed One’s fleshly eye, five colors are found:
the color blue, the color yellow, the color red, the color black, and the color white.
The Blessed One’s body hairs grow individually from each pore.
Wherever these body hairs are set, that area is blue—deep blue, serene, beautiful, and like the color of an *umā* flower.
Beyond that, it is yellow—bright yellow, golden-colored, serene, beautiful, and like the color of a *kaṇikāra* flower.
Both of the Blessed One’s eye-sockets are red, beautifully red, lovely, beautiful to behold, like *indagopaka* insects.
In the middle, they are black, beautifully black, not coarse, pure, lovely, beautiful to behold, like *addāriṭṭhaka* seeds.
Beyond that, they are white, beautifully white, bright, radiant, lovely, beautiful to behold, like the stars of healing herbs.

With that natural fleshly eye of his, which is included within his own physical form and produced by past deeds of wholesome conduct, the Blessed One sees for a league all around, both by day and by night.
Even when there is darkness endowed with four factors— when the sun has set, it is the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight,
there is a dense thicket of forest, and a great black cloud has arisen— he still sees.
Even in such darkness, which is endowed with these four factors, he sees for a league all around.
There is no wall, door, rampart, mountain, bush, or creeper that is an obstruction to his seeing forms.
If he were to take a single sesame seed as a sign and drop it into a cartload of sesame seeds, he would pick up that very same sesame seed.
Thus the Blessed One’s ordinary fleshly eye is completely purified.
In this way, the Blessed One is possessed of vision even by means of the fleshly eye.
How is the Blessed One possessed of vision even by means of the divine eye?
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate;
he understands how beings fare according to their kamma, [knowing]:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind..."
These beings were possessed of wrong view, revilers of the noble ones, holders of wrong views, and undertakers of actions based on wrong views;
with the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings were possessed of good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
“...endowed with these qualities, not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view,
they— upon the breakup of the body, after death— have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye,
purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate.
He understands beings according to their karma.
And if the Blessed One so desired, he could see one world-system, he could see two world-systems,
he could see three world-systems, he could see four world-systems, or he could see five world-systems.
He might see ten world-systems; he might see twenty world-systems; he might see thirty world-systems;
he might see forty world-systems; he might see fifty world-systems; he might see a hundred world-systems;
he might see a small thousandfold world-system; he might see a medium two-thousandfold world-system.
He would see a thousandfold world system; he would see a ten-thousandfold world system; he would see a great thousandfold world system;
indeed, he would see as far as he might wish.
Thus pure is the Blessed One’s divine eye.
Thus the Blessed One is possessed of vision by means of the divine eye.
How is the Blessed One possessed of vision by means of the eye of wisdom?
The Blessed One possesses great wisdom, broad wisdom, joyous wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom, and is skilled in the analysis of wisdom.

One whose knowledge is fully blossomed, who has attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), who has reached the four grounds of self-confidence, who possesses the ten powers, the bull among men, the lion among men, the elephant among men, the thoroughbred among men, the steed among men—possessing infinite knowledge, infinite majesty, and infinite fame; wealthy, possessing great riches, and endowed with wealth;
the leader, the trainer, the one who persuades, the one who makes things known, the one who inspires reflection, the one who causes one to see, and the one who inspires confidence.
For the Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path;
he is the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path; and his disciples now dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.

For the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen. He has become the eye, he has become knowledge, he has become the Dhamma, he has become the Brahma. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.
There is nothing unknown to that Blessed One, nothing unseen, nothing uncomprehended, nothing not realized, and nothing not touched by his wisdom.
With respect to the past, the future, and the present, all phenomena in every aspect come within the range of the vision of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Whatever there may be that is called "to be understood" (neyya) and ought to be known—whether for one’s own benefit, for the benefit of others, or for the benefit of both;
whether a benefit pertaining to the present life or a benefit pertaining to future lives; whether a shallow meaning or a profound meaning;
whether a hidden meaning or a concealed meaning; whether a meaning that is yet to be inferred or a meaning already established; whether a faultless meaning or a state free from defilement.
Whether it be the meaning of the literal sense, the meaning of purification, or the ultimate meaning—all that revolves within the Buddha’s knowledge.
The Blessed Buddha’s knowledge is unimpeded regarding the past, unimpeded regarding the future, and unimpeded regarding the present.
All bodily action of the Blessed Buddha conforms to his knowledge.
All verbal action ...
all mental action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, follows after his knowledge.
To the extent that there is the knowable, to that extent there is knowledge; to the extent that there is knowledge, to that extent there is the knowable.
Knowledge has the knowable as its limit, and the knowable has knowledge as its limit.
Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, nor is there a path of the knowable beyond knowledge.
These phenomena stand as mutual limits for one another.

Just as when two caskets are placed together in perfect contact, the lower casket does not overstep the upper one, nor does the upper casket overstep the lower one, but they both stand with their limits coinciding;
even so, the range of the object (neyya) and the knowledge (ñāṇa) of the Buddha, the Blessed One, stand with their limits coinciding.

As far as the range of the object extends, so far extends the knowledge; as far as the knowledge extends, so far extends the range of the object. Knowledge has the range of the object as its limit; the range of the object has knowledge as its limit.
Knowledge does not proceed by overstepping the knowable, nor is there a path of the knowable that exists beyond knowledge;
these phenomena stand as mutual limits.
The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, proceeds regarding all phenomena.
All phenomena are dependent upon the advertence of the Buddha, the Blessed One; they are dependent upon his wish, dependent upon his attention, and dependent upon the arising of his consciousness.
The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, extends toward all beings.
The Blessed One knows the underlying tendencies of all beings, he knows their latent dispositions, he knows their conduct, and he knows their inclinations.

He knows; he discerns beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good disposition and those of bad disposition, those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct, and those who are capable and those who are incapable.
The world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, revolves within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge.
Just as whatever fish and turtles there are, even including the *timitimiṅgala*, move about within the great ocean;
even so, the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, moves about within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge.
Just as whatever winged creatures there are, even including the *garuḷa* Vainateyya, move about in the regions of space; [so too does this world move within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge].
In the same way, even those who are equal to Sāriputta in wisdom move only within a fraction of the Buddha’s knowledge.
The Buddha’s knowledge stands surpassing and pervading the wisdom of gods and humans.
Even those wise kṣatriyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics who are subtle and skilled in the doctrines of others—
Like those who pierce a hair-tip, they move about as if splitting apart the various speculative views with the weapon of wisdom.
Having repeatedly formulated their questions, they approach the Tathāgata and ask about matters that are hidden and concealed.
Yet those questions, once spoken, are indeed answered by the Blessed One—fully explained with their underlying reasons and decisively resolved.
They fall short of the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One alone outshines them there, namely, by means of wisdom.
Thus the Blessed One is possessed of vision even through the eye of wisdom.
How is the Blessed One possessed of vision through the Buddha-eye?

Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, the Blessed One saw beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes, those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties, those of good disposition and those of bad disposition, those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct; and he saw some who perceive the fear of blame regarding the world beyond.
They dwell while some do not see the danger of blame regarding the world beyond.
Just as in a bed of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses, some of those blue, pink,
or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged within the water, nourished therein;
Some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water,
grow in the water, and remain level with the water; some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water,
grow in the water, and stand rising above the water, unsullied by the water.
In the same way, the Blessed One, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw beings with little dust on their eyes and those with much dust on their eyes;
those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties; those of good disposition and those of bad disposition; those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct;
some dwelling perceiving fear in the fault of the world beyond, and others dwelling not perceiving fear in the fault of the world beyond.
The Blessed One knows:

“This person is of a lustful temperament, this one is of a hateful temperament, this one is of a deluded temperament, this one is of a discursive temperament, this one is of a faithful temperament, and this one is of an intellectual temperament.
For the person of a lustful temperament, the Blessed One gives a discourse on foulness.
The Blessed One teaches the cultivation of loving-kindness to a person of hateful temperament;

he establishes a person of deluded temperament in brief instruction, in questioning, in hearing the Dhamma at the proper time, in discussion of the Dhamma at the proper time, and in living with teachers;
and he teaches mindfulness of breathing to a person of discursive temperament.

For a person of faithful temperament, the Blessed One explains the inspiring signs: the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, the excellence of the Dhamma, the noble practice of the Saṅgha, and his own virtues.
For a person of intellectual temperament, the Blessed One explains the sign for insight: the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, and the aspect of non-self.
“Just as one standing on the summit of a rocky mountain...”
Just as one who, with eyes all around, might look upon the people from every side;
even so, O wise one, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, you possess universal vision.
"Free from sorrow, look upon the people overwhelmed by sorrow,
who are overcome by birth and old age.
Thus did the Blessed One, the possessor of vision, behold with the Buddha-eye.
In what way is the Blessed One possessed of the eye through the universal eye?
"Universal eye" refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutañāṇa*).
The Blessed One is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, attained to, fully attained to, and equipped with omniscient knowledge.
“There is nothing here that he has not seen,
nor anything unperceived or unknown;
he has directly known all that is to be known.”
“The Tathāgata is the All-Seeing One by that [vision].
Thus the Blessed One is “possessed of vision” even by means of the all-seeing eye—
just as one who possesses vision is seen.
"Having dispelled all darkness" means: having shaken off, thoroughly shaken off, abandoned, completely abandoned, and dispelled all darkness— namely, the darkness of lust,
the darkness of hatred, the darkness of delusion, the darkness of conceit, the darkness of views, the darkness of the defilements, and the darkness of misconduct—
which causes blindness, causes lack of vision, causes ignorance, obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna.
"Having made it clear and brought it to non-existence" means having dispelled all darkness.
"He alone has found delight."
The Blessed One is "one" (ekoti) by virtue of his going forth; he is one in the sense of being without a second; he is one in the sense of the abandoning of craving;

he is one as one who is utterly free from lust; he is one as one who is utterly free from hatred; he is one as one who is utterly free from delusion; he is one as one who is utterly free from defilements;
he is one as one who has traveled the path that goes alone; and he is one as one who has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
In what way is the Blessed One alone by virtue of what is called "going forth"?
While still young, with black hair, endowed with the excellence of youth and in the prime of life,
the Blessed One abandoned his circle of kinsmen and everything else, leaving behind his parents who were weeping with tearful faces and lamenting against their will.
Having severed the impediment of household life, having severed the impediment of wife and children, having severed the impediment of relatives,
having severed the impediment of friends and companions, having severed the impediment of hoarding, having shaved off his hair and beard, having donned saffron robes,
having gone forth from the home into homelessness, and having attained a state of possessionlessness, he wanders alone.
He dwells, moves about, conducts himself, protects, maintains, and sustains himself— in this way,
the Blessed One is "one" by way of the designation of renunciation.
How is the Blessed One "one" in the sense of being without a second?
Having thus gone forth, he dwells alone in remote forest lodgings in the wilderness and jungle, which are quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, hidden away from men,
and suitable for retreat. He wanders alone, goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone,
enters the village alone for alms, returns alone, sits alone in private, and practices walking meditation alone.
He wanders alone, dwells alone, moves about, conducts himself, protects, preserves, and maintains himself—
thus the Blessed One is "one" in the sense of being without a second.
How is the Blessed One "one" in the sense of the abandoning of craving?
Thus, dwelling alone, without a companion, diligent, ardent, and resolute, exerting the great effort on the bank of the Nerañjarā River at the foot of the Bodhi tree,
you shattered Māra, the dark Namuci, the kinsman of negligence, along with his host;
you abandoned, dispelled, brought to an end, and utterly eliminated the spreading, clinging net of craving.
“With craving as his companion,
a person wanders through the long course of saṃsāra,
from this state of existence to another state of existence.”
One does not transcend saṃsāra.
Having known this danger—
that craving is the origin of suffering—
“Free from craving, without grasping,
mindful, let the bhikkhu wander.
Thus the Blessed One is one in the sense of the abandoning of craving.
In what sense is the Blessed One "one who has entirely transcended lust"?

He is one because lust has been abandoned; he is one because hatred has been abandoned, thus he is "one who has entirely transcended hatred"; he is one because delusion has been abandoned, thus he is "one who has entirely transcended delusion"; he is one because the defilements have been abandoned, thus he is "one who is entirely free from defilement.
In what sense has the Blessed One "gone the path traveled by the One"? He is one.

The "one-way path" is said to be the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
"The one-way path that leads to the seeing of the destruction of birth, the compassionate one who seeks the welfare of others understands."
"By this path those of old crossed over;
those who will cross and those who are crossing the flood do so by this same way.
Thus the Blessed One has gone upon the path traveled by only one; therefore, he is "one."
How is it that the Blessed One alone awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment? Why is he called "alone"?
"Enlightenment" (bodhi) refers to the knowledge in the four paths—the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, inquiry, insight, and right view.
By means of that knowledge of enlightenment, the Blessed One awakened [to the truth]: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
He awakened to the fact that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering";
he awakened to the fact that "all phenomena are non-self";
he awakened to the fact that "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," and so forth.
He awakened to: “With birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be”;
he awakened to: “With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease” …pe… he awakened to:
“With the cessation of birth, aging-and-death ceases.”
He awakened to: "This is suffering";
he awakened to: "This is the origin of suffering";
he awakened to: "This is the cessation of suffering."
He awakened to: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering”;
he awakened to: “These are the taints” ...
[and so on] ... he awakened to: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.”
“These phenomena are to be fully understood,” he awakened to;
“… are to be abandoned”;
“… are to be developed.”
He awakened to what is to be realized;
he awakened to the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact;
he awakened to the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the five aggregates of clinging.
He awakened to the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the four great elements;
he awakened to the fact that "whatever is subject to arising,
all that is subject to cessation."
Alternatively, whatever is to be awakened to, fully awakened to, awakened to again,
thoroughly awakened to, attained, touched, and realized— all that he awakened to, fully awakened to, awakened to again, thoroughly awakened to,
rightly awakened to, attained, touched, and realized by means of that knowledge of enlightenment.
Thus the Blessed One alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; thus he is "alone.
"He attained delight":
he attained, reached, arrived at, touched, and realized the delight of renunciation, the delight of seclusion, the delight of peace, and the delight of enlightenment.
Alone he found delight.
Therefore the Elder Sāriputta said:
"In the world with its devas..."
Just as one with sight,
having dispelled all darkness,
alone has attained delight.
To that Buddha, the unattached and such-like one,
who had come to the assembly without guile— I,
among many here who were bound, [paid homage].
"I have come with a question:
'The Buddha, the Unattached, the Tādi'.

"Buddha" refers to that Blessed One who is self-become (*sayambhū*), without a teacher, who by himself fully awakened to the truths regarding phenomena previously unheard, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers (*bala*).
In what sense is he "Buddha"?
He is Buddha because he has awakened to the truths;
he is Buddha because he awakens the world.
He is called "Buddha" because of his omniscience,
he is called "Buddha" because of his all-seeing vision,
and he is called "Buddha" because he is not to be led by others.
He is called "Buddha" because of his all-pervading wisdom;
he is called "Buddha" because of the destruction of the taints;
he is called "Buddha" because of being unstained.
The Buddha is one who has completely transcended lust;
the Buddha is one who has completely transcended hatred;
the Buddha is one who has completely transcended delusion.
He is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from defilement;
he is called "Buddha" because he has gone the path traveled by only one;
he is called "Buddha" because he alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
He is "Buddha" because of being devoid of non-intelligence and because of the attainment of intelligence.
This name "Buddha" was not given by his mother, nor by his father,
nor by his brother.
It was not done by her sister,
nor by friends and colleagues,
nor by kinsmen and blood relations.
This was not done by recluses or brahmins, nor was it done by deities.
This is the realization and designation attained at the root of the Bodhi tree by the Blessed Buddhas, simultaneously with the acquisition of omniscient knowledge: namely, "Buddha."
That Buddha.
"Unattached" (asita) refers to two dependencies:
the dependency of craving and the dependency of views.
What is the basis of craving?
Whatever is delimited, encompassed, bounded, grasped, and claimed as "mine" by what is termed craving—namely:
"This is mine; this is for me; this much is mine; to this extent is mine; my forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles."
She covets, through the power of craving, rugs and coverlets, male and female slaves, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares;
fields and lands, silver and gold; villages, towns, royal capitals, kingdoms, and provinces;
treasuries and granaries—even the entire great earth—and as far as the hundred-and-eight modes of the wandering of craving.
This is the dependence on craving.
What is the dependence on views?
It consists of the twenty-based personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), the ten-based wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), and the ten-based extreme-view (antaggāhikā diṭṭhi).
Whatever view such as this there may be— this being a resort of views, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a writhing of views, a fetter of views,
a seizing, a grasping, an adherence, a misapprehension, a wrong path, a false course, falsity,
a sectarian stand, a perverted seizing, a perverted grasping, a perverted distortion, a wrong seizing: "in what is not thus..."
The grasping at things as they truly are, to the extent that there are sixty-two positions of views—
this is the reliance on views.
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, the reliance on craving has been abandoned and the reliance on views has been relinquished.
Because he has abandoned dependence on craving and relinquished dependence on views, the Blessed One is not attached to the eye, nor to the ear, the nose, the tongue,
the body, or the mind; he is not attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, clans,
assemblies, dwellings, gains, fame, praise, pleasure, robes, almsfood, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for the sick.

the sense-sphere realm … the fine-material realm … the immaterial realm … existence in the sense sphere … existence in the fine-material realm … existence in the immaterial realm … existence with perception … existence without perception … existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception … one-constituent existence … four-constituent existence … five-constituent existence … the past … the future … the present …

"Not dependent, not relying, not clinging, not approaching, not adhering, not attached, not intent upon, having gone out from, having escaped from, being liberated from, and dissociated from phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, or cognized; he dwells with a mind free from boundaries"—thus is the Buddha "unattached.
The Blessed One is "suchlike" (tādi) in five ways: [he is suchlike in his bodily conduct, his verbal conduct, his mental conduct, his livelihood, and his demeanor].
He is "such" (tādī) because he is the same toward the agreeable and the disagreeable; he is "such" because he has abandoned [them]; he is "such" because he has crossed over [them];
he is "such" because he is liberated [from them]; he is "such" by way of that description.

How is the Blessed One "such" toward the agreeable and the disagreeable? The Blessed One is the same in gain and the same in loss; he is the same in fame and the same in disrepute; he is the same in praise and the same in blame; he is the same in pleasure and the same in pain.
Some might smear his arm with perfume, while others might carve his arm with an axe;
yet in this one there is no lust, and in that one there is no aversion— one who has abandoned both attraction and repulsion, who has transcended exaltation and depression,
and who has surmounted compliance and hostility.
Thus the Blessed One is "such" (tādī) regarding the desirable and the undesirable.
How is the Blessed One "such" because he has cast off [defilements]?

The Blessed One’s lust has been cast off, vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished; his hatred… delusion… anger… resentment… [has been cast off, vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished].
... hypocrisy ... insolence ... envy ... avarice ... deceit ... craftiness ... obstinacy ...
aggression ... conceit ... arrogance ... vanity ... negligence ... all defilements ...
all misconduct ... all distresses ... all fevers ... all torments ... all unwholesome volitional formations have been vomited up, cast out, abandoned, and relinquished.
In this way, the Blessed One is one who has crossed over; thus he is "one of such a nature. How is the Blessed One one who has crossed over?

The Blessed One has crossed over the flood of sensual desire, he has crossed over the flood of existence, he has crossed over the flood of views, he has crossed over the flood of ignorance. He has crossed over, has emerged from, has gone beyond, has transcended, and has passed entirely across the entire path of saṃsāra. Thus he is "one of such a nature."

Thus he has completed his residence [in the training], practiced the course of conduct, reached the goal, traversed the path, attained the ultimate limit, protected the holy life, achieved the supreme vision, developed the path, abandoned the defilements, and penetrated the unshakable.
He has realized cessation. Suffering has been fully understood by him; its origin has been abandoned; the path has been developed; cessation has been realized.

That which was to be directly known has been directly known; that which was to be fully understood has been fully understood; that which was to be abandoned has been abandoned; that which was to be developed has been developed; that which was to be realized has been realized.
Thus, with the cross-bar lifted, the trench filled in, the pillar uprooted, and the gate thrown open— he is noble, with banner lowered,

with burden laid down, detached, having abandoned the five factors, endowed with the six factors, guarded by the single guard, possessed of the four supports, having shaken off individual dogmatic assertions,
having utterly relinquished seeking, with untroubled intention, with the bodily formations stilled, well-liberated in mind, and well-liberated in wisdom.
The Kevalin, the one who has lived the holy life, the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—
he neither accumulates nor diminishes;
having ceased accumulating and diminishing, he stands firm, neither abandoning nor grasping.
Having abandoned [them], he stands; he neither binds together nor scatters. Having settled, he stands; he neither fans out nor fans in.
Having fanned out, he stands, established because he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha), and the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training.
He stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue; he stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of concentration;

he stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom; he stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of liberation; he stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
he stands having fully realized the truth; he stands having transcended agitation; he stands having exhausted the fire of the defilements.
He stands firm; he stands firm by way of non-wavering; he stands firm having undertaken the task; he stands firm by way of resorting to liberation;
he stands firm in the purification of loving-kindness; he stands firm in the purification of compassion; he stands firm in the purification of sympathetic joy;
he stands firm in the purification of equanimity; he stands firm in ultimate purification; he stands firm in the purification of non-identification; [he stands firm] because of liberation.
He stands; he stands because of his contentment; he stands at the limit of the aggregates; he stands at the limit of the elements;

he stands at the limit of the sense bases; he stands at the limit of destinations; he stands at the limit of rebirths; he stands at the limit of rebirth-linking; he stands at the limit of existence; he stands at the limit of saṃsāra;
he stands at the limit of the cycle of becoming; he stands in his final existence; he stands in his final physical body.
The Blessed One stands firm, bearing his final body:
“This is his last existence;
this is his final physical aggregation.”
“The cycle of birth and death is ended;
for him there is no further becoming.
Thus the Blessed One, having crossed over, is one who is such.
In what sense is the Blessed One "liberated" (muttāvī) and "such-like" (tādī)?
The Blessed One’s mind is liberated, released, and well-released from lust; his mind is [released] from hatred...
from delusion... from anger... from resentment... from contempt... from insolence... from envy... from avarice... from deceit... from fraud... from obstinacy... [and so forth].

His mind is released, liberated, and well-liberated from all undertakings, from conceits, from arrogance, from intoxication, from negligence, from all defilements, from all misconduct, from all distresses, from all fevers, from all torments, and from all unwholesome volitional formations.
Thus the Blessed One is "one who has become liberated," a *tādin*.
In what way is the Blessed One such as he is through that designation?
When virtue exists, the Blessed One is "virtuous"—such is his designation, and thus he is such as he is; when faith exists, he is "faithful"—such is his designation, and thus he is such as he is;

when energy exists, he is "energetic"—such is his designation, and thus he is such as he is; when mindfulness exists, he is "mindful"—such is his designation, and thus he is such as he is; [and] in concentration...
When mindfulness is present, one is designated as "one who is concentrated" because of that; when wisdom is present, one is designated as "one who possesses wisdom" because of that;

when true knowledge is present, one is designated as "one possessing the three knowledges" because of that; when direct higher knowledge is present, one is designated as "one possessing the six direct knowledges" because of that;
and when the ten powers are present, one is designated as "one possessing the ten powers" because of that.
Thus the Blessed One is "such" (tādī) because of that description—
that Buddha who is unattached and such. He is one who does not deceive,
who is counted among the noble ones.
There are three bases for hypocrisy:
the basis for hypocrisy consisting in the acceptance of requisites, the basis for hypocrisy consisting in bodily posture, and the basis for hypocrisy consisting in indirect hinting.
What is the basis for hypocrisy consisting in the acceptance of requisites?
In this case, householders invite a bhikkhu with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. That bhikkhu,
being of evil desires and overcome by longing, out of a desire for more robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,
renounces his robe, renounces his almsfood, and renounces his lodging.
He renounces medicinal requisites for the support of the sick.
He says this:
“What use has a monastic for expensive robes?”
This is appropriate: that a recluse, having picked up rags from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shop, should make them into a patched cloak and wear it.
What need has a recluse for expensive almsfood?
This is appropriate: that a recluse should maintain his life by means of the gleanings of alms-food.
"What need has a recluse for costly lodgings?
It is fitting that a recluse should be a tree-root dweller, a charnel-ground dweller, or an open-air dweller.
What need has a recluse for costly medicinal requisites for the sick?"
"It is appropriate that a recluse should prepare medicine with putrid urine and pieces of green ginger"— thinking thus,
he wears coarse robes, consumes coarse almsfood, uses a coarse resting place,
and uses coarse medicinal requisites for the treatment of illness.
Householders perceive him thus:

"This ascetic is of few wishes, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, and a proponent of the ascetic practices (dhuta). They invite him more and more with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
He speaks as follows:
“Through the coming together of three things, a faithful clansman generates much merit: through the coming together of faith, a faithful clansman generates much merit;
through the coming together of the object to be given, a faithful clansman generates much merit;
through the coming together of those worthy of offerings, a faithful clansman generates much merit.”
"You have this faith, the gift to be given exists, and I am the recipient.
If I do not accept it, you will be excluded from merit; there is no need for me [to receive], yet out of compassion for you alone, I accept.
From that point on, he accepts much robe-cloth, accepts much almsfood, accepts much lodgings, and accepts much medicinal requisites for the sick.
Such frowning, frowardness, scheming, scheming behavior, and a scheming state of mind—
this is the ground for scheming known as the seeking of requisites.
What is the ground for scheming known as deportment?
Here, a certain person who has evil desires and is overcome by craving, with the intention of gaining esteem— thinking, "In this way people will esteem me"—

arranges his walking, arranges his standing, arranges his sitting, and arranges his reclining; he walks with purpose, stands with purpose, sits with purpose, and lies down with purpose, being concentrated.
He walks as if he were concentrated; he stands as if he were concentrated; he sits as if he were concentrated; he lies down as if he were concentrated; he is like one who meditates on the threshold.
Whatever such posing, fixing, adjusting, grimacing, grimacery, hypocrisy, scheming, and scheming-ness there is in the manner of deportment—this is [hypocrisy].
This is the ground for hypocrisy consisting of deportment.
What is the ground for hypocrisy consisting of indirect hinting?
Here, a certain person of evil desires, driven by longing and intent on gaining esteem, thinking, "In this way people will hold me in high esteem," speaks words connected with the noble Dhamma.
"He who wears such a robe is a monk of great authority," he says;
"he who wears such a bowl...
he who wears a bronze dish..."
He carries a needle case;
he carries a water filter;
he carries a key.
"He wears sandals… he wears a waistband… he wears a shoulder-cloth;
that ascetic is one of great influence," he says.
“He whose preceptor is such as this, that ascetic is of great influence,” he says;
“he whose teacher is such as this… he whose co-students are such as these…”
Fellow students… friends… those seen in person…
He says, "He who has shared meals... he who has companions, that ascetic is of great influence";
he says, "He who dwells in such a dwelling, that ascetic is of great influence."
“Whoever dwells in such a two-storied house … dwells in a palace … dwells in a multi-storied building …”
He dwells in a cave… he dwells in a grotto… he dwells in a hut…
He dwells in a gabled house;
he dwells in a watchtower;
he dwells in a multi-storied building.
He dwells in the open air;
he dwells in the assembly hall;
he dwells in the pavilion.
"He dwells at the foot of a tree; that ascetic is of great influence," he says.
Or else, being full of hypocrisy, full of frowning looks, full of deceit, full of chatter, and merely honored for his mouth, he says: "This ascetic is an attainer of such meditative attainments.
He speaks such talk that is profound, obscure, subtle, hidden, supramundane, and associated with emptiness.
Such a frowning face, frowningness, scheming, scheming behavior, and state of being a schemer—this is the basis for scheming known as hinting.
These three bases for scheming have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided by the Buddha, the Blessed One; they are incapable of arising again and have been burnt up by the fire of knowledge.
Therefore, the Buddha is called "without guile"—
he is guileless. This is the meaning of "approached by the multitude."

"Gaṇī" means the Blessed One is a leader of a group (*gaṇī*). He is a "leader of a group" because he is the teacher of a group; he is a "leader of a group" because he is the instructor of a group; he is a "leader of a group" because he sustains the group; he is a "leader of a group" because he exhorts the group;

he is a "leader of a group" because he instructs the group; he is a "leader of a group" because, being confident, he approaches the group; he is a "leader of a group" because he desires to hear from the group.
He lends an ear, applies his mind to understanding—thus he is a leader (*gaṇī*). He leads a group out from the unwholesome and establishes them in the wholesome—thus he is a leader.

He is a leader of a group of monks, a leader of a group of nuns, a leader of a group of laymen, a leader of a group of laywomen, a leader of a group of kings, a leader of a group of kṣatriyas, a leader of a group of brahmins, a leader of a group of vaiśyas.
He was a leader, a leader of the pure assembly, a leader of the Brahma-assembly, a leader of the divine assembly—the leader of the Saṅgha, the leader of the assembly, the teacher of the assembly.
He had come, approached, arrived, and reached the city of Sāṅkāśya; thus he was "the leader who has come without guile."
"Of many bound here":
of many khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans.
"Bound" means those who are bound, attendants, followers, and disciples.
"Of the many who are bound here, some come with a question.
I have come seeking a question; I have come desiring to ask a question; I have come desiring to hear a question."
Thus, there is an arrival by way of a question.
Or else, for those who desire a question, who wish to ask a question, or who wish to hear a question, there may be an arrival, an approaching, a drawing near, and an attendance;
thus, there is an arrival by way of a question.
Alternatively, there is an arrival of a question for you; you too are capable, you are competent to explain and answer what has been asked by me, [thinking] "you will carry this burden.
Thus, there is an arrival by means of a question.
Therefore the Elder Sāriputta said:
“That Buddha, the unattached, the Such-like one,
free from deceit, who has come to the assembly—
[he is the refuge] for many bound here.”
"I have come with a question.
For a monk who feels revulsion [for worldly things] and frequents empty dwellings;
At the foot of a tree, or in a cemetery,
or in mountain caves—
for a bhikkhu who is repelled by the world.
"A bhikkhunī" refers to either an ordinary virtuous bhikkhu or a bhikkhu in training (*sekha*).
"Feeling disgust" means feeling disgust with respect to birth, disgust with respect to aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
[and] disgust with respect to the suffering of hell and the suffering of the animal realm.

by suffering from the realm of hungry ghosts … by human suffering … by suffering rooted in entering the womb … by suffering rooted in remaining in the womb … by suffering rooted in emerging from the womb … by suffering connected to one who is born … by suffering pertaining to one who is born … by self-inflicted suffering … by suffering inflicted by others.

by suffering … by the suffering of suffering … by the suffering of formations … by the suffering of change … by the suffering of eye disease … by the suffering of ear disease … by the suffering of nose disease … by the suffering of tongue disease … by the suffering of body disease … by the suffering of head disease … by the suffering of ear disease … by the suffering of mouth disease … by the suffering of tooth disease.
By suffering ... by coughing ... by spitting ... by nasal catarrh ... by burning fever ... by old age ...
by stomach disease ... by fainting ... by dysentery ... by colic ... by leprosy ... by boils ... by ringworm ...
by consumption ... by epilepsy ... by itch ... by scab ... by herpes ... by rashes ... by blood disorders ...
...by bile ... by urinary diabetes ... by a shoulder-tumor ... by a carbuncle ... by fistula-in-ano ...
by a disease arising from bile ... by a disease arising from phlegm ... by a disease arising from wind ... by a disease arising from a combination of the humors ...
by a disease arising from seasonal change ... by a disease arising from irregular conduct ... by a disease arising from external injury.
… by the suffering born of the ripening of kamma … by cold … by heat … by hunger … by thirst … by the discharge of excrement … by the discharge of urine … by contact with gadflies,

mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things … by the suffering of a mother’s death … by the suffering of a father’s death … by the suffering of a brother’s death … by the suffering of a sister’s death … by the suffering of a son’s death … by the suffering of a daughter’s death.
... because of being disgusted, distressed, ashamed, and repelled by suffering through the loss of relatives, the loss of wealth, the loss of health, the loss of virtue, and the loss of right view—
this is "a bhikkhu who is disgusted."
"An empty seat for one who frequents it":
a seat is that upon which one sits—
a couch, a stool, a mattress, a mat, a piece of leather, a grass mat, a leaf mat, or a straw mat.

That seat is empty, secluded, and isolated from seeing unsuitable forms; it is empty, secluded, and isolated from hearing unsuitable sounds; it is empty, secluded, and isolated from the five unsuitable strands of sensual pleasure.
For one who frequents, resorts to, uses, dwells upon, attends to, and relies upon that secluded seat—it is called "frequenting an empty seat."
"At the foot of a tree or in a charnel ground":
either the foot of a tree itself is the "foot of a tree," or the charnel ground itself is the "charnel ground"— thus,
"at the foot of a tree or in a charnel ground."
"It blows in the caves of the mountains.
Mountains indeed are mountains; ravines indeed are ravines; mountain-caves indeed are mountain-caves.
"Mountain-interstices" refers to mountain-slopes.
Or in caves among the mountains.
Therefore the Elder Sāriputta said:
“For a bhikkhu who feels revulsion...”
Frequenting empty dwellings—
the foot of a tree, a charnel ground,
or caves within the mountains.
In various high and low beds,
how many terrors are there therein,
which a bhikkhu should not be shaken by?
"In a noiseless place" refers to the bedding and seating.
"In high and low beds" means:
"high and low" refers to those that are inferior and superior, or excellent and poor.
"Lying down" refers to lodgings: a monastery, a gabled house, a mansion, a stilt house, or a cave—among such various high and low beds.
"How many terrors are there therein? means: what fears are present there?
*Kīvantō* means how many, crying out, roaring, making noise.
Alternatively, *kīvantō* means how many, how much, how great, how numerous they are.

*Bheravā* refers to lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffaloes, elephants, snakes, scorpions, centipedes, or perhaps thieves, or young men, or those who have committed deeds or those who have not.
"How many terrors are there therein?
'Which, O monk, one should not tremble'—
that is, those terrors which, having seen or heard them, one would not tremble, would not tremble violently, would not tremble all over."
"He would not tremble, he would not be terrified, he would not be cowed, he would not fear, and he would not fall into a state of panic;

he would be fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and not fleeing; he would dwell having abandoned fear and dread, with his hair standing on end gone away"—this is what is meant by "a bhikkhu who would not be shaken."
"Regarding 'a lodging free from noise':
a lodging that is quiet, free from clamor, uninhabited by people, secluded, and suitable for retreat—
this is what is meant by 'a lodging free from noise.'"
Therefore the Elder Sāriputta said:
“In high and low beds,
how many terrors are there therein?”
“Indeed, O bhikkhu, one should not be agitated by noise in one’s lodging.
How many perils are there in the world?
To whatever direction he goes,
those bhikkhus who can endure a remote lodging and seat.
"How many perils are there in the world?
"How many" means how many, how much, how great, how numerous.
"Perils" refers to two kinds of perils: [the internal and the external].
There are manifest dangers and concealed dangers.
What are the manifest dangers?
Lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffalo, elephants, snakes, scorpions, and centipedes; as well as thieves.
Whether they be young men or women, those who have performed meritorious deeds or those who have not, there may arise diseases of the eye, diseases of the ear, diseases of the nose,
diseases of the tongue, diseases of the body, diseases of the head, diseases of the ear, diseases of the mouth, diseases of the teeth, cough, asthma, catarrh, burning sensations,
fever, stomach ailments, fainting, dysentery, colic, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, or scabies.
Rakhasas, vitacchikas, blood, bile, diabetes, carbuncles, and fistulas; diseases originating from bile …pe… cold,
heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things—
these are called manifest perils.
What are the concealed dangers?
They are bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct;
the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the hindrance of doubt; and lust, hatred, and delusion.
Anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy,
aggression, conceit, arrogance, vanity, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all distresses, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations.
These are called concealed perils.
In what sense are they "perils" (*parissaya*)?
They are perils because they overwhelm; they are perils because they lead to decline; they are perils because they dwell therein.
How do they "assail" (parissaya)?
Those perils assail that person, assail him, overcome him, overwhelm him, consume him, and crush him.
Thus they are called "assailing."
Adversities.
How do they lead to decline? These adversities lead to decline by way of creating obstacles for wholesome states.
Of which wholesome states? Of the practice that is right,
the practice that is in accordance [with the Dhamma], the practice that is not contrary, the practice that is non-opposed, the practice that is according to the goal,
the practice that is in conformity with the Dhamma, the fulfillment of the precepts, the guarding of the doors of the sense faculties, and moderation in eating...
Through moderation, through devotion to wakefulness, through mindfulness and clear comprehension, through devotion to the development of the four foundations of mindfulness,
the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—
These things lead to the obstruction and decline of these wholesome states.
Because they lead to decline in this way,
they are called "perils" (parissaya).
How are there dangers lurking therein?
Therein these evil, unwholesome states arise, dependent upon this very personal existence.

Just as creatures that dwell in holes lie in holes, creatures that dwell in water lie in water, creatures that dwell in the forest lie in the forest, and creatures that dwell in trees lie in trees; so too, herein these evil, unwholesome states arise, dependent upon this very personal existence.
In this very way, these evil, unwholesome states arise there, dependent upon the personal existence.
Thus, they are "dangers" (parissaya) because they lie in wait there.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has pupils and a teacher does not dwell in ease or comfort.
And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu with pupils and a teacher dwell in suffering and discomfort?"

"Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, there arise in him evil, unwholesome states that are accompanied by sensual intention and conducive to fettering; these evil, unwholesome states dwell within him and flow into him.
Therefore he is called 'one who has a pupil.
These evil, unwholesome states treat him as they would a pupil."
Therefore, he is called "one together with his teacher.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk has heard a sound with the ear...
[and so on] ...when he has smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...

having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, there arise evil, unwholesome states that are accompanied by intention and are subject to fetters; thus, evil, unwholesome states dwell within him and flow into him.
Therefore he is called "one with pupils.
They treat him [with respect]; evil, unwholesome states do not treat him [with disrespect].
Therefore he is called "one with a teacher."
"In this way, monks, a monk who has pupils and a teacher dwells in suffering and discomfort.
Thus, those which settle there are "perils" (parissaya).
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three internal stains, internal enemies, internal adversaries, internal murderers, and internal foes.
Which three?”
Greed, monks, is an internal stain, an internal enemy, an internal adversary, an internal slayer, and an internal opponent.
Hatred, monks, is an internal stain...
delusion, monks, is an internal stain, an internal enemy, an internal adversary, an internal slayer, and an internal opponent.
These, monks, are the three internal stains, internal enemies, internal adversaries, internal murderers, and internal foes.
Greed gives rise to harm;
greed agitates the mind.
Fear born from within,
people do not perceive it;
being greedy, one does not understand one's true welfare.
The greedy person does not see the Dhamma;
it is blinding darkness then,
when greed overcomes a man.
Hatred gives rise to misfortune;
hatred agitates the mind;
fear born from within—
People do not understand this:
one who is angry does not know the goal;
one who is angry does not see the Dhamma.
Then there is blinding darkness for the man whom hatred overcomes;
delusion is the producer of misfortune.
Delusion agitates the mind;
people do not realize that this fear has arisen from within.
The deluded one does not know the meaning;
the deluded one does not see the Dhamma;
then there is blinding darkness.
"That which delusion overcomes men.
Thus, too, they are called "dwellings" there—
namely, the perils.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Great King, there are three qualities that, arising within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and lack of comfort.
Which three?”

Greed, great king, is a state that, when arising within a person, arises for his harm, suffering, and lack of comfort. Hatred, great king, [is a state that, when arising within a person, arises for his harm, suffering, and lack of comfort].
Delusion, great king, is a state that, when arising within a person, arises for his harm, suffering, and lack of comfort.
"These three qualities, Great King, when arising within a person, arise for his harm, suffering, and lack of well-being:
greed, hatred, and delusion—
these lead a person of evil mind."
"Those born from themselves destroy themselves,
like a fruit that destroys its own rind.
Thus, too, they find their dwelling there.
Dangers.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Lust and hatred originate from this source..."
Dislike, like, and horripilation are born from this;
mental thoughts arise from this,
just as young birds leave the nest.
"Thus they dwell there"—
these are the perils.
"In the world"— that is, in the human world.
How many perils are there in the world?
For one who goes, they see what has not yet been reached.
That which has not yet been reached is called the deathless Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna—
that direction has never been gone to before, nor has it ever been gone to in this long course of time.
It is level, full, and without remainder.
Just as one would carry about a bowl of oil,
so should one guard one's own mind,
yearning for a destination never before reached.
"One who goes toward a direction not previously gone to" means one who advances while going;
thus, "the direction not yet gone to by one who is going.
These are the monks whom he overcomes.
"Whatever perils he might encounter, overcome, be overwhelmed by, be consumed by,
or be crushed"— these perils, O bhikkhu,
he overcomes while dwelling in a remote lodging.

"In a remote place" means: at the edge of a village, at the edge of a field, at the edge of a rock, at the edge of a forest, at the edge of a river, or at the edge of water; wherever there is no plowing or sowing, having passed beyond inhabited areas, in a lodging that is outside the human sphere—this is "a remote bed and seat.
Thus spoke the Elder Sāriputta.
“How many perils are there in the world for one going to an unknown region,
which a bhikkhu must overcome?”
"Upon a lowly bed and seat"—
what would his modes of conduct be,
and what would his spheres of activity be here?
What would be his rules and observances,
for a bhikkhu who is resolute?
What would be his modes of address?
"With what kind of speech, what manner, what form, and what appearance should he be endowed?"—thus he asks regarding purity of speech.
What is purity of speech?
Here, a bhikkhu, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech; he is a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech;

having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people, nor having heard something there, does he repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those people.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united. Delighting in concord, rejoicing in concord, finding joy in concord, he speaks words that bring about concord.
Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech;
he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-reaching, urbane, agreeable to many people, and beloved by many people.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, and speaks what is meaningful.
He speaks as one who proclaims the Dhamma and proclaims the Vinaya; he utters speech that is well-founded, timely, reasoned, measured, and beneficial.
He is endowed with the four modes of verbal good conduct and speaks speech free from the four faults.
He is averse to, abstains from, desists from, has emerged from, is released from, and is liberated from the thirty-two kinds of frivolous talk, dwelling with a mind that is beyond all boundaries.
He speaks on ten topics of discourse, namely: talk on fewness of desires,
talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on the arousal of energy,
talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation, and talk on the foundations of mindfulness.

He speaks on the discourse of the right efforts, the discourse on the bases of psychic power, the discourse on the faculties, the discourse on the powers, the discourse on the factors of enlightenment,
the discourse on the path, the discourse on the fruits,
and the discourse on Nibbāna. He is restrained, vigilant, prepared, guarded, protected, shielded, and self-controlled in his speech.
This is purity of speech.
"May he be endowed with such purity of speech"—
what would his modes of expression be?
“What, indeed, is his resort here?
He asks about the resort: “Of what kind of resort would he be possessed? Of what nature? Of what character?
Of what appearance? There is a resort; there is a non-resort.
What is an improper resort?

Here, someone has prostitutes as a resort, or widows as a resort, or unmarried girls as a resort, or eunuchs as a resort, or bhikkhunīs as a resort, or taverns as a resort; he is closely associated with them.
He dwells in unwholesome association with kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and the disciples of those sects.
Or else he dwells among families that are faithless, lacking confidence, ungenerous, abusive, and insulting;
families that do not desire his welfare, do not desire his benefit, do not desire his comfort, and do not desire his security from bondage for the monks and nuns.
He frequents, associates with, and attends upon such families as those of laymen and laywomen—
this is called an improper resort (*agocara*).
Alternatively, having entered among the houses or set out upon the street, he walks without restraint, looking about at elephants...
He goes looking at horses, looking at chariots, looking at infantry, looking at women, looking at men,
looking at girls, looking at boys, looking at the marketplace, looking at the doorways of houses,
looking upward, looking downward, and glancing about in all directions and intermediate points.
This too is called a non-range.
Or else, having seen a form with the eye, one grasps at its signs and grasps at its secondary characteristics.
On account of which basis... [as before]... [this is called a non-range].

If one dwells with the faculty of the mind unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states might flow in upon him; yet he does not practice for its restraint, he does not guard the faculty of the mind, and he does not achieve restraint over the faculty of the mind—this too is called an improper resort.
Or again, as some worthy recluses and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such frivolous spectacles as these: [the list follows].
Dancing, singing, instrumental music, theatrical performances, storytelling, hand-clapping, drumming, cymbals, clowns, acrobats, outcasts,
reed-pipers, water-splashing, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights,
goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, staff-fights, boxing, and wrestling.
Whether it be military parades, reviews of troops, battle arrays, or the inspection of armies— engaging in such frivolous spectacles as these is called an improper resort. Furthermore,
the five strands of sensual pleasure are also improper resorts.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Monks, do not wander in what is not your own resort, the domain of others.
Monks, for those who wander in what is not their own resort, the domain of others, Māra will find an opportunity; Māra will find a foothold.”
And what, bhikkhus, is the non-range, the alien domain of a bhikkhu?
It is these five cords of sensual pleasure.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … [and so forth].
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
This, monks, is called a monk’s non-range, the domain of others.”
This too is called a non-range.
What is the range?
Here, a bhikkhu does not have prostitutes as his range, nor widows as his range, nor unmarried girls as his range.
He does not frequent the quarters of eunuchs, he does not frequent the quarters of bhikkhunīs, he does not frequent taverns;
he dwells unassociated with kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and followers of other sects, avoiding improper association.

Furthermore, he frequents those families that are faithful and confident, which serve as wellsprings for the Saṅgha, where the yellow robes shine like lamps, and which are cooled by the breeze of the sages.
One who frequents, associates with, and attends upon families that desire the welfare, benefit, comfort, and security of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
this too is called a proper resort.
Alternatively, when a bhikkhu has entered among the houses and is walking along a street, he goes restrained; he does not look at elephants, nor look at horses, nor look at chariots,
nor look at infantry … [and so on] … he does not walk about looking here and there in the various directions—
this too is called a resort.
Or else, when a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs...
[and so on] ...he attains restraint over the mind-faculty—
this too is called the "range."
Or again, just as some worthy recluses and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, dwell not devoted to such frivolous spectacles as these:
namely, dancing, singing, instrumental music... [and so on] ...or the watching of military parades; one who abstains from such frivolous spectacles—this too is called a resort.
The four foundations of mindfulness are the domain.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, move within your own domain, within your ancestral range."
“Bhikkhus, for those who walk in their own range, in their own ancestral domain, Māra will find no opportunity; Māra will find no foothold.
And what, bhikkhus, is the bhikkhu’s range, his own ancestral domain?
It is these four foundations of mindfulness.”
Which four?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, [and] feelings in feelings... [etc.]

He dwells contemplating mind in the mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
This, monks, is called a monk’s own resort, his ancestral domain.
This too is called a resort.
"May he be endowed with such a resort"—
what would his resorts here be?
"What are his rules and observances? means:
"Endowed with what kind of rules and observances would he be? Of what character, of what nature, and of what appearance? Thus he asks about the purity of rules and observances.
What is the purity of rules and observances?
There is both virtue and observance; there is observance that is not virtue.
What is both virtue and observance?

Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
That which therein is restraint, self-control, and non-transgression—
this is virtue (sīla). That which is undertaking [of the precepts]— this is virtue.
That is the vow.
In the sense of restraint it is virtue; in the sense of undertaking it is a vow—this is called both virtue and a vow.
What is austerity that is not virtue?
The eight ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas):

the practice of forest-dwelling, the practice of eating only almsfood, the practice of wearing rag-robes, the practice of using only three robes, the practice of continuous alms-round, the practice of refusing food after the proper time, the practice of sitting meditation, and the practice of accepting whatever seat is offered.
This is called a vow, not virtue.
The undertaking of energy is also called a vow, not virtue:
"Let only skin, sinews, and bone remain; let the flesh and blood dry up in the body."

Thinking, "That which is to be attained through manly steadfastness, manly strength, manly energy, and manly exertion— that shall not be reached without the stabilization of my energy," he uplifts his mind and strives.
Such an undertaking of energy is called a vow, not virtue:
“I will neither eat nor drink;
I will not go out from the monastery.”
"I shall not cast down my gaze as long as the arrow of craving has not been extracted.
Thus he exerts his mind and strives.
Even such an undertaking of energy is called a vow, not virtue.
"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging"—
thus he exerts and strives with his mind.
Even such an undertaking of energy is called a "vow," not "virtue.
"I shall not rise from this seat until...
"...I shall not descend from this walking path until..."
"I shall go out from the monastery… I shall go out from the half-roofed house… I shall go out from the palace…"
A hut… a cave… a grotto…
Huts … gabled houses … watchtowers …
In the upper story … in the pavilion … in the assembly hall …
Thinking, "I will go from the pavilion... or from the foot of the tree until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging," he exerts and strives his mind.
Such an undertaking of energy is called a vow, not virtue.
At this very time of morning, he exerts and strives with the thought: "I will bring forth the noble Dhamma, I will gather it, I will attain it, I will touch it, I will realize it."
Such an undertaking of energy is called a vow, not virtue.
Even at this very time of midday… or at the time of evening… [one undertakes it].
Before the meal … after the meal … during the first watch of the night …
the middle watch...
the last watch...
at night...
In summer...
in the rainy season...
in winter...
In summer … in the first stage of life … in the middle stage of life …
"In the final stage of life, I shall bring forth the noble Dhamma, I shall gather it, I shall attain it, I shall touch it,
I shall realize it"— with such thoughts, one exerts and strives.
Such an undertaking of energy is called a vow (*vata*), not virtue (*sīla*).
This is purity of conduct and observances.
"May I be endowed with such purity of conduct and observances"— what [specific] conducts and observances would these be?
“Of a bhikkhu who is resolute” (*pahitattassa bhikkhuno*).

“Resolute” (*pahitattassa*) means one who has initiated energy, who has attained firmness, who possesses steadfast exertion, who has not abandoned his desire for wholesome states, and who has not laid down his burden regarding wholesome states.

Alternatively, it means one whose mind is directed; he to whom [the mind] is directed for the sake of his own welfare, for the sake of the *ñāya*, for the sake of the *lakkhaṇa*, for the sake of the *kāraṇa*, and for the sake of what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna*).
For one whose mind is directed toward the thought, “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent”;
for one whose mind is directed toward the thought, “All conditioned phenomena are suffering”;
and for one whose mind is directed toward the thought, “All phenomena are non-self.”
“For one whose mind is directed toward ‘with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]’ …pe… for one whose mind is directed toward ‘with birth as condition,
