aging-and-death [arise],’ and for one whose mind is directed toward ‘with the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of volitional formations’ …pe…”
“For one whose mind is directed toward ‘with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death’;
for one whose mind is directed toward ‘this is suffering’ …pe… for one whose mind is directed toward ‘this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’,” [he said].
“For these are the taints,” directed thus...
“This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints,” directed thus;
“These phenomena are to be directly known,” directed thus... [and so forth].
“‘These phenomena are to be realized’—thus for one who is intent;
‘the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact’—thus for one who is intent;
‘the five aggregates subject to clinging’ …”
For one whose mind is directed toward the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the four great elements;
for one whose mind is directed toward the fact that "whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.
"A bhikkhunī" refers to either a bhikkhu who is a virtuous worldling (*puthujjana-kalyāṇaka*) or a bhikkhu who is a trainee (*sekha*).
For a bhikkhu who is resolute.
Therefore the Elder Sāriputta said:
“What would his modes of address be?”
What indeed would be his range here?
What would be his virtues and observances for a bhikkhu who is resolute?”
Having undertaken that training,
being unified, discerning, and mindful—
just as a smith [refines] silver—
"Shake off the impurity from yourself.

Regarding "having undertaken which training": having taken it up, undertaken it, adopted it, fully accepted it, grasped it, handled it, and adhered to it—it is thus "having undertaken which training."
"Unified, mindful, and discerning.

"Unified" means one whose mind is one-pointed, whose mind is undistracted, whose consciousness is not scattered; it is serenity, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and so forth, up to right concentration.
“Nipaka” means one who is prudent, wise, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.
“Sato” (mindful) means mindful by way of four reasons:
when one develops the foundation of mindfulness consisting of contemplation of the body as body, one is mindful;...
He is mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness through the contemplation of feelings … [and so on] … the mind … [and so on] … phenomena as phenomena.
Thus he is called "mindful"—
he is mindful.
When it is asked, "Having undertaken what training?", it asks about the training in higher virtue.
"Unified in mind" (ekodī) asks about the training in higher consciousness;
"vigilant" (nipaka) asks about the training in higher wisdom;
"mindful" (sata) asks about complete purity.
Having undertaken which training, being unified, discerning, and mindful, one shakes off one’s own impurity just as a smith [shakes off] that of silver.
A "smith" is called a goldsmith; "silver" is called natural gold (*jātarūpa*).
Just as a goldsmith blows upon, melts, and purifies even the coarse impurities of gold, and blows upon, melts, and purifies the medium impurities,
and blows upon, melts, and purifies even the subtle impurities; even so, a bhikkhu blows upon, melts, and purifies his own coarse defilements— he abandons them, dispels them,
makes them vanish, brings them to non-existence— and he blows upon, melts, and purifies the medium defilements… and the subtle defilements.
He shakes it off, blows it away, abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end,
and causes it to cease to exist. Or else, a bhikkhu [shakes off] his own stain of greed, stain of hatred, stain of delusion, stain of conceit, stain of views,
stain of defilements, and stain of misconduct— which causes blindness, causes lack of vision, causes lack of knowledge, obstructs wisdom, and belongs to the side of affliction.
He fans it out, fans it thoroughly, blows it away, abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent—namely, that which does not lead to Nibbāna.
Or alternatively, with right view he fans out, fans thoroughly, blows away, abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and makes non-existent wrong view.
With right intention, he [fans out] wrong intention... and so on.
Right speech [abandons] wrong speech;
right action [abandons] wrong action;
right livelihood [abandons] wrong livelihood.
By right effort, [one abandons] wrong effort;
by right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness;
by right concentration, wrong concentration.
By right knowledge, wrong knowledge is blown away,
thoroughly blown away, winnowed out, abandoned, dispelled, brought to an end, and made non-existent. Or else,
by means of the noble eightfold path, all defilements, all misconducts, all anxieties, and all [afflictions] are [blown away].
In the face of all burning fevers and all torments, he blows away, thoroughly purifies,
expels, abandons, dispels, makes an end of, and brings to non-existence all unwholesome volitional formations;
thus, like a smith blowing away the dross from his silver, he cleanses himself of impurity.
Therefore the Elder Sāriputta said:
“Having undertaken what training,
being unified, prudent, and mindful;”
"Just as a smith blows away the impurities from silver, so should one blow away the impurities of oneself.
This is the comfort for one who feels revulsion.
(Sāriputta, said the Blessed One:
For one who frequents empty seats and lodgings,
desiring full enlightenment in accordance with the Dhamma,
I shall explain that to you as I understand it:
"That which is comfortable for one who feels revulsion.

"For one who feels revulsion" means for one who feels revulsion toward birth, toward aging, toward sickness, toward death, toward sorrow, toward lamentation, toward pain, toward grief, toward despair... [and so forth].
"For one who is disgusted, trembling, and ashamed by the suffering of the calamity of wrong views"—
this is "for one who is disgusted.
"That which is comfortable" means that I shall explain that comfortable dwelling.

What is dwelling in comfort? It is right practice, conformable practice, non-contrary practice, unopposed practice, practice according to the goal, practice in accordance with the Dhamma and its principles,
fulfillment of the precepts, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and moderation in eating.
Devotion to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, Nibbāna,
and the practice leading to Nibbāna.
“This is a comfortable dwelling”— that is, this comfort for one who is feeling revulsion.
“Sāriputta,” said the Blessed One.
He addresses that elder by name.
"Bhagavā" is a term of reverence; moreover, he is called "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed passion (*bhagga-rāgo*).
The Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed hatred;
the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed delusion;
the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed conceit.
The Blessed One has destroyed wrong views;
the Blessed One has destroyed thorns;
the Blessed One has destroyed the defilements.
The Blessed One has distributed, shared out, and bestowed the jewel of the Dhamma;
the Blessed One makes an end of existence;
the Blessed One is one whose body is cultivated, whose virtue is cultivated, whose mind is cultivated, and whose wisdom is cultivated.
The Blessed One frequented remote lodgings in forest and jungle tracts—solitary, quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, remote from human habitation, and suitable for retreat;
thus he is the Blessed One. Or, the Blessed One is a partaker of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; thus he is the Blessed One.
Or, the Blessed One is a partaker of the essence of meaning, the essence of Dhamma, the essence of liberation, of higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom; thus he is the Blessed One.
Or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he is a partaker of the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he is a partaker of the eight liberations, the eight bases of direct knowledge, and the nine successive dwellings in attainment;

or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he is a partaker of the ten developments of perception, the ten kasiṇa attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, and the attainments of the foul.

The Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path;

or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the six qualities of a Buddha.

"Bhagavā"—this name was not made by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by friends and companions, nor by kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities;
this is a designation based on liberation, realized at the foot of the Bodhi tree by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, upon the simultaneous acquisition of omniscient knowledge: namely, "Bhagavā."
"Sāriputta," said the Blessed One.
"Or for one who uses a seat and a bed that are empty.
By "seat" is meant that upon which one sits.
A bed, a bench, a mattress, a mat, a piece of hide, a grass mat, a leaf mat, or a straw mat.
A "resting place" refers to lodgings such as a monastery, a gabled house, a mansion, a stilt house, or a cave.
That resting place is empty, secluded, and utterly remote from the sight of unsuitable forms; it is [empty, secluded, and utterly remote] from the hearing of unsuitable sounds... [and so on].
It is empty, secluded, and utterly remote of the five unwholesome strands of sensual pleasure.
For one who uses, resorts to, frequents, and dwells upon that lodging and seat— it is for such a one,
“for one who uses an empty seat and bed.”
"According to the Dhamma for one desiring full enlightenment":
"Full enlightenment" (sambodhi) is said to be the knowledge, wisdom, faculty of wisdom, and power of wisdom within the four paths; ...
[and so on] ... it is the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, inquiry, insight, and right view.

"To one who desires full enlightenment"—that is, to one desiring to awaken to that enlightenment, to awaken after it, to awaken in opposition to it, to awaken thoroughly, to attain it, to touch it, and to realize it. "In accordance with the Dhamma":
what are the factors in accordance with enlightenment?

The right way of practice, the conformable way of practice, the non-contrary way of practice, the unopposed way of practice, the way of practice according to the goal, the way of practice in accordance with the Dhamma,
the fulfillment of moral discipline, guarding the doors of the sense faculties,
moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, and mindfulness and clear comprehension.
These are called the factors in conformity with enlightenment.
Alternatively, insight during the preliminary stage of the four paths is called the factors in conformity with enlightenment.
I shall explain to you that which conforms to the Dhamma for one desiring full enlightenment,
just as those who understand it perceive it. "That" refers to the practice in accordance with the Dhamma leading to enlightenment.
"I shall proclaim" means: I shall proclaim, declare, teach, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and elucidate.

[I shall do so] such that they understand; such that one understanding, one comprehending, one discerning, one penetrating, and one piercing through, does not rely on "it is so" (itihitiha), nor on tradition (itikirāya), nor on hearsay (paramparāya), nor on the authority of the scriptures (piṭakasampadāya), nor on reasoning (takka-hetu), nor on logical deduction (naya-hetu).
"I shall speak of that Dhamma which has been personally realized and directly witnessed through higher knowledge— not by means of mere reflection on modes, nor by approval based on views—
but as I myself understand it, so shall I declare it to you."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For one who feels revulsion, this is what constitutes comfort” (addressing Sāriputta, the Blessed One said).
I shall explain to you, according to my understanding,
how one who desires full awakening should practice the way of Dhamma while using a riding animal, a seat, or a bed.
A wise bhikkhu, mindful and walking within the bounds of restraint, should not fear the five fears:
gadflies and mosquitoes, and creeping reptiles.
Of human contacts and four-footed creatures,
the wise man does not fear these five fears.
"The wise man" (dhīra) means one who is steadfast, learned, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.
The wise person should not fear, tremble, be terrified, be struck with terror, be distressed, or fall into a state of panic regarding the five fears;
rather, he should dwell fearless, undaunted, unafraid, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and free from horripilation.
“The wise one does not fear the five fears:
‘A bhikkhu who is mindful and walks within bounds.
Here, “bhikkhu” refers to either a bhikkhu who is a virtuous worldling or a bhikkhu who is a trainee (sekha).
"Mindful" means mindful for four reasons:
when developing the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body, he is mindful;
[when developing it] in regard to feelings … [and so on].
When one develops the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects with regard to the mind, being mindful—
one is called "mindful."
"One who conducts oneself within bounds" refers to four bounds:
the bound of restraint by virtue, the bound of restraint of the sense faculties, the bound of moderation in eating, and the bound of devotion to wakefulness.
What is the bound of restraint by virtue?

Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
Reflecting on his state of internal corruption, he moves within the boundary of internal restraint of virtue and does not break the limit—this is the boundary of restraint of virtue.
What is the culmination of restraint of the sense faculties?
Here, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Whatever [unwholesome states] might arise on that account... [as before].
He attains restraint over the faculty of the eye.

Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having touched a tangible object with the body... having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
When he dwells with this faculty of the mind well-restrained, covetousness and dejection—those evil, unwholesome states—do not arise.
If unwholesome states were to flow in through the mind-faculty, he practices for its restraint; he guards the mind-faculty and achieves restraint over the mind-faculty.
Reflecting upon the Discourse on the Burning, he conducts himself within the limits of restraint of the faculties and does not break the boundary—this is the limit of restraint of the faculties.
What is the culmination of moderation in eating?

Here, a bhikkhu reflects wisely as he takes food: not for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for the sake of physical beauty or attractiveness, but only for the maintenance and preservation of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life;
thinking, "Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling."
Reflecting on food as being like axle-oil, a salve for a wound, or the flesh of one's own son, he conducts himself within the limits of moderation in eating and does not transgress those boundaries;
this is the limit of moderation in eating.
What is the limit of devotion to wakefulness?
Here, a bhikkhu purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the day;
he purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the first watch of the night;
during the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot placed upon the other.

Mindful and clearly comprehending, having attended to the perception of rising, he rises during the last watch of the night and purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
Reflecting upon the dwelling of the "One Fortunate Night," he conducts himself within the limits of the practice of wakefulness and does not transgress its boundary.
"This is the culmination of devotion to wakefulness"—
thus a bhikkhu is one who dwells mindfully and within bounds regarding gadflies,
mosquitoes, and creeping reptiles.
"Bites" refers to the brown flies.
"Those that fall upon" refers to all flies.
For what reason are all flies called "those that fall upon"?
They fly up again and again and devour them;
for that reason, all flies are called "adhipātaka.
Reptiles are called "ahī" (snakes).
Of biting and stinging creatures, of reptiles, of human contacts, and of quadrupeds.
"Human contacts" refers to thieves, or youths, or those who have committed an offense, or those who have not.
They might question that bhikkhu with a problem, or engage him in debate, or revile him, or abuse him, or become angry,
or become enraged, or injure him, or cause him injury, or harm him, or cause him harm, or strike him, or cause him to be struck, or inflict some form of violence upon him—
from whatever human source such violence may arise.
Human contact.
"Four-footed animals" refers to lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, wolves, buffaloes, and elephants.
These might maul a bhikkhu, devour him, injure him, harm him, afflict him, torment him, kill him, wound him, or cause him injury.
"Harm from four-footed creatures" refers to any fear arising from four-footed beings,
such as humans or other quadrupeds.
Thus the Blessed One said.
“A wise monk, mindful and walking within his boundaries, should not fear the five fears:
gadflies and mosquitoes, snakes, and creeping reptiles.”
"Of human touches and four-footed creatures.
One should not be terrified even by those who follow other doctrines,
even after seeing their many horrors.
Furthermore, the one who seeks what is wholesome should overcome other dangers;
even upon seeing their many terrors, he should not be terrified by those belonging to the faction of others.
Those who are hostile to the Dhamma are said to be anyone—excluding those who share the same Dhamma—who lack confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
They might question a bhikkhu, or engage him in debate, or revile him, or abuse him, or become angry with him, or become excessively angry;
they might harm him, or cause him injury, or inflict suffering upon him, or cause him excessive suffering; they might kill him, or attempt to kill him, or do him physical harm.
"Upon seeing or hearing many terrifying things, they would not tremble, would not shake, would not be shaken all over;
they would not be afraid, would not be terrified, would not be frightened, would not be cowed, would not fear, and would not fall into terror.
They would dwell fearless, undismayed, unafraid, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and dread, and with their hair standing on end gone."
One should not be terrified even upon seeing the many horrors of those who follow other doctrines.
Furthermore, one who seeks what is wholesome should overcome other perils as well— those that must be mastered, conquered, overwhelmed, exhausted, and crushed.
“Dangers” means two kinds of dangers:
manifest dangers and concealed dangers … [as before] … thus it is “wherein one dwells.”
Regarding "obstacles":

"seeking what is wholesome" means seeking and searching for the right practice, the conformable practice, the non-opposing practice, the uncontradicted practice, the practice that accords with the goal...
[and so on] ...the Noble Eightfold Path, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna.
"By one who is seeking, dangers must be overcome, mastered, overwhelmed, exhausted, and crushed"— thus,
as one seeking what is wholesome, one may further overcome other dangers.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
One should not be afraid even of those who follow the highest Dharma,
even after seeing their many terrors;
rather, one should overcome other [more formidable] things.
“A wise person seeking the wholesome should endure afflictions:
touched by the touch of illness or by hunger,
one should patiently endure cold and heat.”
Thus, when touched by these in many ways,
though having no home, one should exert firm energy and perseverance.
"Touched by the touch of affliction and by hunger" means this.
"Affliction-contact" is said to be "disease-contact.
He would be touched, overcome, afflicted, and possessed by disease-contact;
he would be touched, overcome, afflicted, and possessed by eye-disease.
by disease of the ear,
by disease of the nose,
by disease of the tongue,
He might be afflicted, overcome, distressed, and possessed by a bodily disease... [and so on] ...or by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things.
"Hunger" is said to mean starvation.
"Afflicted, oppressed, overwhelmed, and possessed by the touch of illness and hunger"—
thus he is afflicted by the touch of illness and hunger.
"He would endure cold and heat."
"Cold" is cold for two reasons:
it is either cold due to the disturbance of the internal elements, or it is cold due to external temperature.
"Hot" is hot for two reasons: [it is either hot due to the disturbance of the internal elements, or it is hot due to external temperature].
It is cold because of an internal disturbance of the elements, or it is hot because of external temperature; thus, "cold and heat.
"He should endure" means he should be patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things.
He should be one who is by nature patient with harsh and offensive paths of speech, and with bodily feelings that have arisen which are painful,
sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening—
he should endure cold and heat.
"Thus touched by them in many ways, he is homeless": "Touched by them"—
meaning that he would be touched, overcome, afflicted, and possessed by those things, namely, by the touch of illness, by hunger, by cold, and by heat— thus he is "touched by them."
"Bahudhā" means that he would be touched, overcome, deluded, and possessed by many kinds of forms;
thus, "touched by those in many ways.
"Anoka" means that he does not provide a place for consciousness accompanied by volitional formations.
"Without abode.
Alternatively, it is called "without abode" because one does not provide an opportunity for bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, or mental misconduct.
Thus, touched by those [afflictions] in many ways,
he who has no home should exert firm energy and perseverance.
"Energy and perseverance" refers to that mental application of energy, the undertaking, the striving, the exertion, the effort, and the endeavor.
Exertion, enthusiasm, non-retrogression, steadfastness, fortitude, unrelenting perseverance, non-abandonment of desire, non-abandonment of the burden,
the uplifting of the burden, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, right effort.
One should make firm one's energetic exertion.
One should make energy firm, one should make exertion firm; one should be of firm undertaking, of steadfast undertaking—this is "one should make energy and exertion firm.
Thus the Blessed One said.
“Afflicted by the touch of illness and by hunger,
he should endure cold and heat;
though touched by these in many ways, being homeless, he should remain.”
One should exert firm energy.
One should neither commit theft nor speak falsehood;
one should touch all beings, both those that tremble and those that are stable, with loving-kindness.
When one recognizes that the mind has become defiled,
one should dispel it as being on the side of darkness.
One should neither commit theft nor speak falsehoods.

"He does not commit theft": here a bhikkhu, having abandoned taking what is not given, abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart pure and free from stain—thus he "does not commit theft.

"He should not speak falsehood": here a bhikkhu, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech; he is a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world—thus [he speaks].
One should neither commit theft nor speak falsehood.
One should touch with loving-kindness all beings, both those that move and those that are stationary. "Loving-kindness" (*mettā*) means:

that which is loving-kindness toward sentient beings, the state of being loving-kind, the state of practicing loving-kindness; friendliness, the state of being friendly, the state of practicing friendliness; the desire for their welfare, compassion, non-malice, non-harming, and the wholesome root of non-hatred.
"Those who are 'thirsting' (tasā)" refers to those for whom craving has not been abandoned and for whom fear and terror have not been abandoned.
For what reason are they called "thirsting"?
Because they tremble, are terrified, are anxious, are afraid, and fall into a state of panic.
They are called "the trembling" (tasa) because of that [fear].
They are called "the steady" (thāvara) because they have abandoned the trembling of craving and have abandoned fear and terror.
For what reason are they called "the steady"?
They do not tremble, they do not fear, they do not become terrified, they do not dread, and they do not fall into panic;
for that reason they are called "the steady" (thāvara). Thus it is said:
"By means of loving-kindness, touch both the trembling and the steady."

"One should touch and pervade with loving-kindness both the moving and the stationary; having pervaded with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—one should dwell [thus]":
this is "touching the moving and the stationary with loving-kindness.
"When one discerns the turbidity of the mind" refers to this.
Whenever it is said "the mind": that which is called *citta*, *mano*, *mānasa*, *hadaya*, *paṇḍara*, *mano*, *manāyatana*, *manindriya*, *viññāṇa*, *viññāṇakkhandha*,
and the corresponding *manoviññāṇadhātu*— by means of bodily misconduct, the mind becomes turbid, agitated, stirred up, disturbed, shaken, wavering, and unpeaceful.
By way of verbal misconduct … [and so on] … by way of mental misconduct … by way of lust …
... by hatred ...
by delusion ...
by anger ...
... by malice ...
by hypocrisy ...
by spite ...
... by envy ...
by stinginess ...
by deceit ...
... by deceitfulness ...
by stubbornness ...
by contentiousness ...
by conceit … by overweening pride … by intoxication …
... by negligence ...
by all defilements ...
by all misconduct ...
...from all distresses ...
from all fevers ...
from all torments ...
The mind becomes turbid, stirred up, agitated, disturbed, shaken, wavering, and unpeaceful by all unwholesome volitional formations.
"One should discern the turbidity of the mind" means:
one should know, understand, discern, thoroughly discern, and penetrate the state of turbidity of the mind.
When one should recognize that the mind has become turbid,
one should dispel it, thinking, "This belongs to the faction of the Dark One.
The "Dark One" (kaṇha) is Māra, the dark overlord, the internal Namuci, the kinsman of the heedless.

"The side of darkness, the side of Māra, the snare of Māra, the trap of Māra, the bait of Māra, the domain of Māra, the abode of Māra, the range of Māra, the bond of Māra—one should abandon it, dispel it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease.
In this way too, one should dispel what is "the side of darkness.
Or alternatively, "the side of darkness" means the side of Māra, the side of the unwholesome, which leads to the arising of suffering, results in suffering, and conduces to hell.
"Leading to rebirth in the animal realm or leading to the sphere of hungry ghosts— one should abandon it,
dispel it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease.
In this way, too, one should dispel that which belongs to the dark side.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One should neither commit theft nor speak falsehood;
one should touch with loving-kindness all beings, both those that tremble and those that are stable.”
When one recognizes that the mind has become defiled,
one should dispel it, thinking, "This is on the side of the dark.
One should not come under the sway of anger and arrogance.
One should stand having dug up even their very roots;
whether it be pleasant or unpleasant,
you will certainly experience the consequences.
"One should not come under the power of anger and arrogance.
"Anger" is that which is resentment and hostility toward the mind...
[and so on] ...fury, impetuosity, and mental dissatisfaction.
"One who is conceited" means that here someone despises another on account of birth, or clan, or... [as before] ...or some other basis.

"One should not come under the sway of anger and conceit" means one should not come under the sway of both anger and conceit; one should abandon anger and conceit, dispel them, bring them to an end, and cause them to cease.
One should not fall under the power of anger and pride;
one should remain having dug up even their very root.
What is the root of anger?

Ignorance is its root, improper attention is its root, the conceit "I am" is its root, moral shamelessness is its root, moral fearlessness of wrongdoing is its root, and restlessness is its root— this is the root of anger.
What is the root of overweening pride?
Ignorance is its root, improper attention is its root, the conceit "I am" is its root, moral shamelessness is its root, moral fearlessness is its root, and restlessness is its root—
this is the root of overweening pride.
Even having excavated their roots, one remains [established].
"Having dug out, pulled up, torn out, and completely eradicated the root of anger and arrogance, having abandoned it, dispelled it, brought it to an end, and rendered it non-existent,
one would stand firm, remain established"— thus, having dug out even their root, one would stand. Then,
whether toward what is pleasant or what is unpleasant, one will surely overcome existence.

Now, "atha" (then) is the conjunction of words, the meeting of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of consonants, and the sequential order of words—this is what "atha" means.
There are two kinds of "piya" (dear): [the dear as an object and the dear as a feeling].
Either beings or formations.
Which beings are dear?

Here, those who wish for his welfare, who wish for his benefit, who wish for his comfort, who wish for his security from bondage—whether they be mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friend, minister, kinsman, or blood relative.
These beings are dear.
Which conditioned phenomena are dear?
Agreeable forms, agreeable sounds…
Odors … tastes … tangibles—
These formations are dear.
"Not dear" refers to two kinds of things that are not dear:
either beings or formations.
Which beings are disagreeable?
Here, those who wish him harm, wish him ill, wish him discomfort, wish him lack of security from bondage, and wish to deprive him of life—
these beings are disagreeable.
What are the formations that are unpleasant?
They are unpleasant forms, unpleasant sounds, odors, tastes, … [and tactile objects].
Tangible objects— these formations are unloved.

"Addhā" is a categorical statement, a statement free from doubt, a statement free from uncertainty, a statement free from duality, a statement free from ambiguity, a definitive statement, an unequivocal statement, and a stabilizing statement.
"Certainly.
Whether it be pleasant or unpleasant, certainly you, sir, would overcome it.

Whether it be the pleasant and unpleasant, the agreeable and disagreeable, pleasure and pain, joy and grief, or the desirable and undesirable—whether by overcoming them or by mastering them, you would certainly overcome them.
Whether it be pleasant or unpleasant, one will surely have to endure it.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One should not come under the sway of anger and arrogance.”
Even having dug up their very roots, one might stand firm;
whether it be pleasant or unpleasant,
you will surely experience the consequences of your actions.
Placing wisdom foremost and possessing noble joy,
one should suppress those dangers;
one should overcome aversion while lying down in a secluded place.
"One should overcome the four states conducive to lamentation,
placing wisdom foremost and possessing noble joy. Here, "wisdom" (*paññā*) refers to that which is wisdom,
understanding, investigation, thorough investigation, investigation of phenomena … [and so forth].
Non-delusion is right view.
"Placing wisdom foremost" means that here someone proceeds having placed wisdom at the front; one who has wisdom as his banner, wisdom as his standard, and wisdom as his sovereign;
one who abounds in investigation, abounds in scrutiny, abounds in observation, abounds in thorough observation, who dwells in clarity, and whose conduct is directed toward that.
“Abounding in that, making that heavy, inclining toward that, leaning toward that, tending toward that, intent upon that, having that as its governing principle.
Thus too, one has wisdom placed foremost.
Or else, while walking, one understands: “I am walking”; while standing, one understands: “I am standing”; while sitting...
Or he understands, "I am sitting," or when lying down, he understands, "I am lying down";
or in whatever way his body is disposed, he understands it accordingly.
Thus too, having placed wisdom foremost.
Or else, he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, bowl, and inner robes;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; and he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating.
"He acts with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus too, one places wisdom foremost.
"Beautiful rapture" refers to the joy and gladness that arise by way of the recollection of the Buddha.

"Wholesome rapture": the rapture and gladness that arises by way of recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of the deities, mindfulness of breathing, mindfulness of death, mindfulness occupied with the body, and mindfulness of peace—
this is called "wholesome rapture."
"Placing wisdom foremost, with beautiful rapture, one should ward off those perils. Regarding "perils":
there are two kinds of perils.
There are manifest dangers and concealed dangers...
[as above] ...these are called manifest dangers...
[as above] ...these are called concealed dangers... [as above].
"Thus they lie there"—
these are the perils.
"One should suppress those perils."
"One would suppress, overcome, overwhelm, exhaust, and crush those dangers"—
thus, one suppresses those dangers.
"One should endure discontent while lying on a remote bed."
"Discontent" means that which is discontent, the state of discontent, lack of delight, lack of enjoyment, longing, and agitation.
"In regard to a remote lodging" means that one should endure, overcome, master, exhaust, and subdue any discontent regarding remote lodgings or any among the various higher wholesome states;
thus, "one should endure discontent in regard to a remote lodging."
"One should endure the four states of lamentation":
one should endure, withstand, overcome, surmount, exhaust, and subdue the four things that cause lamentation— thus, "one should endure the four states of lamentation."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Placing wisdom foremost, with sublime joy,
one should suppress those dangers.”
"One should overcome discontent while lying on a remote bed;
one should overcome the four states of lamentation.
"What indeed would I eat? Where indeed would I eat?"
"Alas, how painful it will be to lie down tonight!
A trainee who wanders without a home should dispel such thoughts that lead to lamentation."
"What shall I eat? How shall I eat? "What shall I eat?
means: "Shall I eat rice, or sour gruel, or parched grain, or fish, or meat?"—this is "what shall I eat."
"Where will they eat? Where shall I eat—in a khattiya family, a brahmin family, a vessa family, or a sudda family?"—"What shall I eat?
Where shall I eat?"—"Alas, how painful it was for them to sleep!
Where will they sleep tonight? They slept painfully on a wooden plank, or on a mat, or on a piece of hide, or on a bed of grass, or on a bed of leaves, or on a bed of straw."
"Where shall I lie down comfortably this coming night— on a couch, or a chair, or a mattress, or a pillow; in a monastery, or a gabled house, or a palace, or a tower,
or a cave?"— "Alas, I have slept well, but where indeed shall I sleep tonight?"—
these are thoughts that lead to lamentation.
He thinks these thoughts: two thoughts connected with almsfood, and two thoughts connected with lodgings.
"Lamentable" means fit for lamenting, fit for wailing;
these thoughts are lamentable.
"The trainee should discipline himself, wandering without a home.
Why is the "trainee" (sekha) so called?
Because he trains (sikkhati).
One in training. And what does one train in?
One trains in higher virtue, one trains in higher mind, and one trains in higher wisdom.
What is the training in higher virtue? ... [as before] ...
this is the training in higher wisdom.
One trains by being mindful of these three trainings, knowing them, seeing them, reviewing them, and resolving the mind upon them.
He trains; he trains resolving with faith, exerting energy, establishing mindfulness, concentrating the mind, and understanding with wisdom;

he trains directly knowing what is to be directly known, fully understanding what is to be fully understood, abandoning what is to be abandoned, developing what is to be developed, and realizing what is to be realized.
Realizing it, he trains, practices, practices thoroughly, and trains having undertaken it.
For that reason, he is called a "learner" (sekha).

For the sake of discipline, for the sake of counter-discipline, for the sake of abandoning, for the sake of calming, for the sake of relinquishment, and for the sake of subsiding, one should train in higher virtue, one should train in higher mind, and one should train in higher wisdom.
One should train while reflecting upon these three trainings; one should train knowing them...
[as before] ...one should train realizing what is to be realized; one should practice, practice thoroughly, and having undertaken them, conduct oneself accordingly.
The trainee should discipline himself.
Regarding "one who wanders without a home":
how does one become a wanderer with a home?
In this case, someone is possessed of the obstacle of family, the obstacle of the group, the obstacle of the dwelling,
the obstacle of robes, the obstacle of almsfood, the obstacle of lodgings, or the obstacle of medicinal requisites for the sick.
Thus, one is a wanderer who dwells in a home.
How does one live as a wanderer without a fixed abode? Here, a bhikkhu is not possessed of the impediment of families, nor the impediment of social groups, nor the impediment of dwellings,
nor the impediment of robes, nor the impediment of almsfood, nor the impediment of lodgings, nor is he possessed of the impediment of medicinal requisites for use in sickness.
Thus he is one who wanders without a fixed abode:
“Some have gone to Magadha, some have gone to Kosala,
and others to the land of the Vajjis.”
Like deer, the bhikkhus wander without a flock;
they dwell without a fixed abode.
Excellent is good conduct, excellent is well-practiced conduct.
Excellent is the constant dwelling without a home;
asking about the goal and acting with circumspection—
this is the state of a recluse for one who possesses nothing.
Let the trainee discipline himself, wandering without a fixed abode.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“What shall I eat? Where shall I eat?”
“Alas, O Best One, how painful will be my sleep tonight!
A trainee who wanders without a home should dispel these thoughts that lead to lamentation.”
Having obtained food and clothing at the proper time,
he should know moderation for the sake of contentment in this world;
guarded among those things and restrained in his conduct within the village, he—
Even if one is reviled, one should not utter harsh speech.
Having obtained food and clothing at the proper time—
where "food" refers to boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat— one should use them.
And there are robes to wear:
linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and bark-cloth.
Having obtained food and clothing, one dwells at ease.
Having obtained a robe and having obtained almsfood, one does not act through scheming, nor through flattery, nor through hinting, nor through belittling others,
nor through the pursuit of gain by means of gain; nor through the gift of wood, nor the gift of bamboo, nor the gift of a bowl,
nor the gift of flowers, nor the gift of fruit, nor the gift of bathing facilities, nor the gift of bath powder.
Not by the giving of clay, not by the giving of tooth-sticks, not by the giving of water for rinsing the mouth,
nor by flattery, nor by bean-soupery, nor by servility, nor by fawning, nor by geomancy, nor by low arts,
nor by the science of bodily marks, nor by the science of astrology, nor by acting as a messenger, nor by going on errands, nor by running messages on foot.
Not by means of medical practice, nor by exchanging alms-food for alms-food, nor by giving in exchange for gifts;
rather, having obtained, acquired, attained, found, and received it in accordance with the Dhamma and with justice—
having obtained food and clothing at the proper time.
“He should know the measure for the sake of contentment here.
“He should know the measure” means he should know the measure by two reasons:
either from the standpoint of receiving or from the standpoint of using.
How does one know the proper measure in receiving?

Even when little is being given, one receives for the sake of the family’s prosperity, for the protection of the family, and out of compassion for the family; even when much is being given, one receives only such robes as are necessary for the body and such alms-food as are necessary for the belly.
In this way, one knows the proper measure in receiving.
How does one know the proper measure through use?

Reflecting wisely, he uses the robe only for protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and only for the purpose of concealing the private parts.

Reflecting wisely, he uses almsfood neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for the sake of physical beauty nor for embellishment, but only for the maintenance and preservation of this body, for the allaying of hunger, and for supporting the holy life.
"Thus, I shall terminate old feeling and not give rise to new feeling; so that there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.

Reflecting thus with wise consideration, he makes use of lodgings merely for protection from cold, for protection from heat, for protection from contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and merely for the purpose of warding off the perils of the climate and for enjoying seclusion.
He uses the requisite of medicine as a support for the sick with wise reflection, solely for the purpose of warding off arisen afflictive feelings and for the sake of supreme non-affliction.
In this way, he knows the proper measure from the perspective of enjoyment. Thus it is said:
"He should know the measure."
By these two reasons, one should know the measure, understand it, discern it, and penetrate it— thus,
"he should know the measure. Herein, it is for the purpose of satisfaction.

Here, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe and speaks in praise of being content with any kind of robe; he does not engage in improper search for the sake of a robe, nor is he anxious if he does not obtain one.
Having obtained a robe, he uses it without being attached, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger in it and understanding the escape from it.
Furthermore, by virtue of that contentment with any kind of robe, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever there is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—that monk is said to be established in the ancient, foremost, noble lineage.
Furthermore, a monk is content with whatever almsfood he receives; through such contentment with whatever almsfood he receives...
He speaks in praise of it, yet he does not engage in improper search for the sake of almsfood; if he does not obtain almsfood,
he is not distressed, and if he obtains almsfood, he enjoys it without being attached, infatuated, or clinging to it, seeing the danger in it and possessing the wisdom of escape.
And by means of that contentment with whatever almsfood may be obtained, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and ever mindful—
it is such a person who is called a bhikkhu established in the ancient, primordial noble lineage.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of lodging and speaks in praise of being content with any kind of lodging;
he does not resort to improper search for the sake of a lodging, and when he does not obtain a lodging, he is not anxious;
and when he obtains a lodging, he is unattached, uninfatuated, and unpossessed by it, seeing the danger in it.
He uses [the lodging] with wisdom regarding the escape from it;
and by means of that contentment with whatever lodging he receives, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—
This is called a bhikkhu who stands firm in the ancient, foremost noble lineage.
Furthermore, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick, and he speaks in praise of being content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick;
yet he does not, for the sake of medicinal requisites for the sick, [seek them improperly].
He does not engage in inappropriate searching; he is not anxious when he has not obtained requisites for the sick, medicines, and provisions;
and when he has obtained requisites for the sick, medicines, and provisions, he uses them without being attached, infatuated, or clinging, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
And because of that contentment with the various requisites for the sick, such as medicines and provisions, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—it is said of him:
"This bhikkhu stands in the ancient, foremost lineage of the noble ones."
He should know the measure here for the sake of contentment.
Thus guarded among them, he moves with restraint in the village.
"Guarded among them" means he is guarded, protected, shielded, and restrained regarding robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
In this way too he is guarded among them.
Or alternatively, he is guarded, protected, shielded, and restrained with regard to the sense bases;
in this way too he is guarded among them.
"Restrained in conduct in the village" means: in the village he is restrained, self-controlled, prepared, guarded, protected, and restrained;
thus, being guarded among those [people], he is "restrained in conduct in the village.
Even when provoked, he does not utter harsh speech.
If one is reviled, censured, disparaged, struck, reproached, or abused with harsh and cruel words, one should not respond in kind nor retort;
when another reviles, one should not revile in return; when another is angry, one should not be angry in return;
when another quarrels, one should not quarrel in return; one should not engage in strife, one should not engage in brawling, and one should not engage in contention.
One should not engage in dispute; one should not engage in contention. One should abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence quarreling, brawling, strife, dispute, and contention.
One should be aloof from, detached from, and fully withdrawn from quarreling, brawling, strife, dispute, and contention;
one should have emerged from them, escaped them, and be liberated from them, dwelling with a mind for which there are no boundaries. Thus it is said.
Even when provoked, one should not utter harsh speech.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having obtained food and clothing at the proper time...”
He should know the proper measure here for the sake of contentment;
guarded among those [people] and restrained in his conduct in the village,
even when provoked, he should not utter harsh speech.
With downcast eyes and not fidgeting with his feet,
devoted to meditation and wide awake,
having attained equanimity, he is composed in self.
"He cuts off speculative views and worry.
How does one have wandering eyes? "With downcast eyes and not fidgety with the feet.
How does one have wandering eyes?
Here, a certain bhikkhu is fickle-eyed; he is possessed of fickleness of eye, thinking,

"I shall see what has not been seen" and "I shall transcend what has been seen," and goes from monastery to monastery, from park to park, from village to village, from town to town, from city to city,
from kingdom to kingdom, and from country to country, on long journeys and unstable wanderings.
And he is intent on looking at forms.
In this way too, his eye is cast outward.
Or else, a bhikkhu who has entered among the houses and is walking along a street goes unrestrained, [looking at] an elephant...

He goes looking here and there, looking at the horses, looking at the chariots, looking at the infantry, looking at women, looking at men, looking at boys, looking at girls, looking at the market stalls,
looking at the doorways of houses, looking upward, looking downward, and glancing about in every direction.
In this way too, he has a wandering eye.
Or else, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, grasps at its general appearance and grasps at its secondary details.
Because his faculty of the eye remains unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might assail him.

If, when he has gone out among families, covetousness and dejection should flow in upon him regarding forms cognizable by the eye, he does not practice for its restraint; he does not guard the eye-faculty;
he does not achieve restraint over the eye-faculty.
In this way too, his eye is distracted.
Or again, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, remain devoted to such frivolous spectacles as these:
namely, dancing, singing, instrumental music, theatrical performances,

storytelling, hand-clapping, drumming, cymbals, tambourines, acrobatics, mimes, clowns, elephant fights, horse fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights, fighting with staves, boxing, wrestling, sham-fights, roll-calls, camp-signals, bugle-calls, military reviews, maneuvers, encirclements, battle-arrays, and the like.
Bullfights, cockfights, quailfights, stick-fighting, boxing, wrestling,
mock combat, military parades, reviews of troops, and the inspection of battle arrays—
this is what is meant by "having the eye cast outward."
How does one not have wandering eyes?
Here, a certain bhikkhu is not fickle of eye, nor possessed of fickle eyes;
he does not go from monastery to monastery, from park to park, or from village to village with the thought, "I shall see what has not been seen" or "I shall transcend what has been seen."
He does not travel from town to town, from city to city, from kingdom to kingdom,
or from province to province on long journeys or unsettled wanderings, nor is he intent upon seeing forms.
In this way, too, his gaze is not cast about.

Or else, a bhikkhu who has entered among the houses and is walking along a street goes restrained; he does not look at an elephant... [and so on] ...he does not walk looking about here and there in the various directions.
In this way too, his eye is not cast about.
Or else, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs... [and so on] ...he attains restraint over the faculty of the eye.
In this way too, he does not have a wandering eye.

Furthermore, he abstains from such devotion to idle sightseeing as that of certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten meals provided by the faithful, frequent elephant battles, cavalry battles, chariot battles, infantry battles, military parades, or the reviewing of troops.
He abstains from such pursuits of idle sightseeing.
Thus he does not have a wandering eye—
this is one with downcast eyes.
Nor is he fidgety with his feet.
How is one restless with the feet?

Here, a certain bhikkhu is restless with the feet; being possessed of restlessness with the feet, he wanders from monastery to monastery... [and so on] ...he is devoted to long journeys and unstable wandering for the sake of seeing sights.
In this way too, one is restless with the feet.

Alternatively, a bhikkhu, even within the monastery compound, is fickle with his feet; possessed of such fickle foot-movements, he goes from one courtyard to another, or from one dwelling to another, agitated and with an unpeaceful mind, neither for a purpose nor for a reason,
and engages in talk about "becoming this" or "becoming that."
In this way, too, one is fidgety with the feet.
"Not fidgety with the feet" means that one should abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence the habit of fidgeting with the feet; one should be free from fidgeting with the feet.
He would dwell abstaining, refraining, having gone forth from, having escaped from, being liberated from, and dissociated from [sensual pleasures], with a mind free from boundaries;
he would delight in seclusion, rejoice in seclusion, be devoted to internal tranquility of mind, not neglecting meditation,
endowed with insight, cultivating empty huts, a meditator who rejoices in meditation, devoted to unity, and regarding his own goal as most important.
"With downcast eyes and not fidgety with the feet;
devoted to jhāna, one who is wide awake.
As for "devoted to jhāna": one is devoted to jhāna for two reasons.
He is engaged, devoted, intent, and committed to the arising of the first jhāna that has not yet arisen; or he is engaged, devoted, intent,
and committed to the arising of the second jhāna… the third jhāna… that have not yet arisen.
"He is engaged, devoted, intent, and fully committed to the arising of the fourth jhāna.
Thus, too, he is "devoted to jhāna.
Alternatively, he cultivates, develops, and repeatedly practices the first jhāna once it has arisen.
Or he pursues, develops, and cultivates the second jhāna that has arisen… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna.
Thus too is one devoted to meditation.
"Of one who is wide awake": here, during the day, a bhikkhu purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting;
during the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.

He purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the middle watch of the night; he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising;
and having risen during the last watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
"Devoted to meditation, for one who is wide awake,
having begun with equanimity, with a concentrated mind. Here,

"equanimity" (upekkhā) refers to that equanimity, the state of looking on, the state of looking on closely, the evenness of mind, the tranquility of mind, and the neutrality of mind found in the fourth jhāna.

"Of concentrated mind": that stability, steadfastness, firmness, non-distraction, non-diffusion of the mind, the state of a non-diffused mind, serenity, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and right concentration.
"Having undertaken equanimity, of concentrated mind":
in the fourth jhāna, having undertaken equanimity, one whose mind is one-pointed, whose mind is undistracted, whose mind is non-diffused.
Having established equanimity and being concentrated in self,
he cuts off the tendency toward discursive thought and remorse.
"Discursive thoughts" refers to the nine types of applied thought (vitakka).
Sensual thought, thought of ill will, thought of cruelty, thought of relatives, thought of the country, thought of immortality,
thought associated with seeking gain, thought associated with honor and praise, and thought associated with not being despised—
these are called the nine thoughts.

The underlying tendency toward sensual perceptions is the basis for thoughts of sensuality; the underlying tendency toward ill-will perceptions is the basis for thoughts of ill-will; the underlying tendency toward cruelty perceptions is the basis for thoughts of cruelty.

Alternatively, ignorance is the basis for conjecture, discursive thought, and intention; improper attention is the basis; the conceit "I am" is the basis; lack of moral dread is the basis; and restlessness is the basis. As for remorse (*kukkucca*):
remorse regarding the hands is remorse, remorse regarding the feet is remorse, and remorse regarding both hands and feet is also remorse.

Worry: the perception of what is improper as proper, the perception of what is proper as improper; the perception of what is unseasonable as seasonable, the perception of what is seasonable as unseasonable;
the perception of what is blameless as blameworthy, the perception of what is blameworthy as blameless.
Such worry, the state of worrying, the tendency to worry, mental remorse, and mental scrupulousness—this is called worry.
This is called worry.
Furthermore, worry arises for two reasons: mental remorse and mental anguish, due to what has been done and what has not been done.
How does remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish arise through what has been done and what has not been done?
“I have committed bodily misconduct; I have failed to perform bodily good conduct”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.
“I have committed verbal misconduct... [and so forth].
“Mental misconduct was committed by me...
Killing was committed by me; abstaining from killing was not practiced by me”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental distress.
“Taking what is not given was committed by me... [and so forth].
I have committed sexual misconduct;
I have committed false speech;
I have committed divisive speech.
Harsh speech has been committed by me… frivolous chatter has been committed by me… covetousness has been committed by me…
“Malice was committed by me… wrong view was adopted by me, right view was not adopted by me”— thus there arises remorse, mental regret, and mental vexation.
In this way, remorse, mental regret, and mental vexation arise from what has been done and what has not been done.
Or else, there arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish, thinking: "I was not one who fulfilled my duties regarding the precepts";
"I did not guard the doors of the sense faculties";
"I was not moderate in eating."
“I am not devoted to wakefulness,” … “I am not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension,” … “The four foundations of mindfulness have not been developed by me,” …
“I have not developed the four right strivings,” … “I have not developed the four bases of psychic power,” … “I have not developed the five faculties,” …
“I have not developed the five powers,” … “I have not developed the seven factors of enlightenment,” … “I have not developed the noble eightfold path. …
“Suffering has not been fully understood by me,” … “The origin of suffering has not been abandoned by me,” … “The path has not been cultivated by me. …
“Cessation has not been realized by me”—thus arises remorse, mental regret, and mental anguish.

Speculation cuts off remorse. One should cut off, sever, eradicate, utterly destroy, abandon, dispel, bring to an end, and cause the disappearance of both speculation and the tendency toward speculation, as well as remorse. One should cause them to cease to exist.
One should cut off speculative views and remorse.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“With downcast eyes and not fidgety with his feet,”
Devoted to meditation, one who is wide awake,
having established equanimity with a concentrated mind,
should cut off the tendency toward discursive thought and remorse.
Rejoicing with mindfulness when reproved by words,
one should break down the barrenness within fellow practitioners of the holy life;
one should utter wholesome speech, but not in excess.
One should not intend for the sake of worldly rumor.

When reproached by words, one who possesses mindfulness rejoices. "Reproached" means that preceptors, teachers, those with the same preceptor, those with the same teacher, friends, those seen together, those who have shared meals, or companions reproach him.
“Friend, this is unbecoming for you; this has not been attained by you; this is unsuitable for you; this is contrary to your virtue.

Having established mindfulness, one would welcome that admonition, rejoice in it, delight in it, approve of it, desire it, accept it, long for it, yearn for it, and ardently aspire to it—just as a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of ornaments, and having washed their heads, might welcome a garland of blue lotuses or a garland of jasmine.
Just as one who, having obtained a garland of *adhimuttaka* flowers, would receive it with both hands, place it upon the head— the highest limb— and rejoice,
exult, be glad, approve, desire, accept, aspire, long for,
and yearn for it; even so, having established mindfulness, one should rejoice, exult, be glad, approve, desire, accept, aspire, long for, and yearn for that exhortation.
One who sees faults, who speaks with censure, and who is wise— such a person one should regard as the guardian of treasures.
One should associate with such a wise person.
For one who associates with such a person,
it becomes better, not worse.
One should advise and instruct,
and restrain one from what is unwholesome;
for such a person is dear to the virtuous.
“He becomes unloved by the wicked.
Thus rebuked with words, the mindful one should rejoice; he should break up the barrenness toward his fellow practitioners in the holy life.
“Fellow practitioners in the holy life” means those who share the same formal acts, the same recitation of the scriptures, and the same training.
"He breaks the barrenness toward fellow practitioners of the holy life.
He should break the state of a heart wounded toward fellow practitioners of the holy life, the state of being like a wasteland;

he should break the five kinds of mental barrenness, he should break the three kinds of mental barrenness; he should break, shatter, and utterly destroy the barrenness of lust, the barrenness of hatred, and the barrenness of delusion. Thus it is said.
"One should break through the barrenness toward one's fellow practitioners in the holy life.
One should utter speech that is wholesome and not excessive.

This means: one should utter speech arisen from knowledge; one should utter speech that is connected with the goal, connected with the Dhamma, timely, well-reasoned, and measured—one should utter such speech, one should let it go forth.
One should utter speech that is wholesome.
"Not beyond the limit" (*nātivelam*):
"limit" (*velā*) refers to two limits—
The time-limit for speech and the moral-limit for speech.
What is the time-limit for speech?

One should not speak words that have transgressed the [proper] time, one should not speak words that have transgressed the [proper] occasion, nor should one speak words that have transgressed both the time and the occasion.
One should not speak; one should not speak words when the time has not arrived; one should not speak words when the occasion has not arrived;
one should not speak words when the proper time and occasion have not arrived.
"He who, indeed, when the time has not arrived..."
And he speaks excessively;
thus he lies defeated,
like the cuckoo’s own offspring.
This is the time-limit.
What is the virtue-limit?
One who is lustful should not speak; one who is hateful should not speak; one who is deluded should not speak; one should not speak false speech.

One should not speak; one should not speak malicious speech, one should not speak harsh speech, one should not speak idle chatter—one should not utter it, should not say it, should not speak it, should not illuminate it, should not express it.
This is the boundary of virtue.
One should utter speech that is wholesome and not excessive.
One should not intend for the sake of worldly talk. "People" refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, gods, and humans.

One should not intend, nor arouse the thought, nor arouse the intention, nor arouse the mental attention, for the sake of public talk, disparagement, blame, reproach, ill-repute, or the destruction of one's reputation; nor for the sake of failure in virtue, failure in conduct, failure in view, or failure in livelihood.
One should not intend for the sake of worldly gossip.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Though reproached by words, the mindful one should rejoice.”
One should break through the barrenness toward fellow practitioners of the holy life;
one should utter wholesome speech, not excessively,
and should not intend to engage in the kind of talk that is the way of worldly people.
Furthermore, there are five stains in the world,
for the removal of which the mindful one should train:
in visible forms, in sounds, and likewise in tastes,
“One should overcome passion for scents and for touches.
Now, as for the word “atha” (then/furthermore):
it is a conjunction of words, a meeting of words, a completion of words, a combination of syllables, a smoothness of phonemes, and a sequential order of words.
Now, "five kinds of dust" refers to the dust of visible forms, the dust of sounds, the dust of odors, the dust of tastes, and the dust of tangibles.
"Passion is dust; it is not called 'dust' in the sense of a particle."
"Passion" is a designation for "dust.
Having utterly abandoned this dust, the wise dwell in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
Defilement is not called "dust," nor is it called "dirt" ...
they dwell in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
Delusion is not called dust, nor is it called grit;
... they dwell in the teaching of the One Free from Dust.
The world: the world of the states of misery, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of the aggregates, the world of the elements, and the world of the sense bases— these, moreover,
are the five stains in the world,
for the restraint of which one who is mindful trains.
They yearn for passion for forms, passion for sounds, passion for odors, passion for tastes, and passion for tangibles. "Mindful" refers to that which is mindfulness,

constant mindfulness, specific mindfulness, mindfulness, the state of remembering, the state of bearing in mind, the state of not forgetting, the state of not losing track, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, and the path of the single way— this is called mindfulness.
One who is endowed with this mindfulness, fully endowed with it, approached with it, fully approached with it, possessed of it, fully possessed of it,
and equipped with it, is called "mindful.
As for "training," there are three trainings:
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
What is the training in higher virtue? ... [as above] ...
this is the training in higher wisdom.
"Of those for whose discipline one who is mindful trains":

a mindful person, for the sake of the discipline, the removal, the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishment, and the calming of lust for forms, lust for sounds, lust for odors, lust for tastes, and lust for tangibles— even the higher morality— [trains].
One should train in the higher mind and one should train in the higher wisdom; one should train while attending to these three trainings, one should train while knowing them...
[and so on] ...one should train, practice, fully practice, and conduct oneself by undertaking that which is to be realized, while realizing it.
“Those who, being mindful, train for discipline:
they should overcome passion for forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and tangibles.
To overcome passion for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles means to endure it, to withstand it, to master it, to overwhelm it, to exhaust it, and to crush it.
One should conquer passion for forms, sounds, and likewise tastes, smells, and touches.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, there are these five stains in the world..."
Those who, being mindful, train for discipline,
should conquer passion for forms, sounds, and likewise tastes, smells, and tangibles.
Having removed desire for these phenomena,
a mindful bhikkhu with a well-liberated mind,
examining the Dhamma correctly at the proper time, [attains peace].
"Becoming one-pointed, he should dispel the darkness" (thus said the Blessed One).
"Having removed desire for these phenomena."
"In these" means in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. "Lust" refers to that which is lust for sensual pleasures,

passion for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, fever for sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, clinging to sensual pleasures, the flood of sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasures, the grasping of sensual pleasures— and so on—
up to the hindrance of lust for sensual pleasures.
"Having removed desire for these phenomena":
having removed, thoroughly removed, abandoned, dispelled, made to vanish, and brought to non-existence the desire for these phenomena—
this is "having removed desire for these phenomena."
"A bhikkhu who is mindful and whose mind is well-liberated.
Regarding "bhikkhu": it may be a bhikkhu who is a virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), or a bhikkhu who is still in training (*sekha*).
Regarding "mindful" (*satimā*): that which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness... [as above] ...right mindfulness, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the path of the single way.
This is called mindfulness.
One who is endowed with this mindfulness, fully endowed with it … [as before] … he is called mindful.
"A bhikkhu who is mindful and whose mind is well-liberated":
for one who has attained the first jhāna, the mind is released, liberated, and well-liberated from the hindrances;
for one who has attained the second jhāna, the mind is released, liberated, and well-liberated from applied and sustained thought.
For one who has attained the third jhāna, the mind is released, liberated, and well-liberated from rapture;
for one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the mind is released, liberated, and well-liberated from pleasure and pain;

for one who has attained the base of infinite space, the mind is released, liberated, and well-liberated from the perception of form, the perception of sensory impingement, and the perception of diversity.
The mind of one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness is released, liberated, and well-liberated from the perception of the base of infinite space;

the mind of one who has attained the base of nothingness is released, liberated, and well-liberated from the perception of the base of infinite consciousness; the mind of one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is released, liberated, and well-liberated from the perception of the base of nothingness.

The mind of a stream-enterer is liberated, freed, and well-liberated from the view of a personal body, doubt, and misapprehension of rules and observances, as well as from the underlying tendencies of views and doubt, and from the defilements associated with them.
The mind of a once-returner is liberated, freed, and well-liberated from coarse underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill will, as well as from the defilements associated with them.

The mind of a non-returner is freed, liberated, and well-liberated from the fetter of sensual lust accompanied by latent tendencies, the fetter of ill will accompanied by latent tendencies, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to ill will, and from the defilements associated with them.

The mind of an arahant is freed, liberated, and well-liberated from lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to ignorance, from the defilements associated with them, and from all external signs.
Thus, a bhikkhu is mindful and his mind is well-liberated.
“Investigating the Dhamma properly at the right time”:
“At the right time” means that when the mind is agitated, it is the time for serenity; when the mind is concentrated, it is the time for insight.
“At the right time he uplifts the mind...”
Furthermore, he restrains it;
at the proper time he gladdens it,
and at the proper time he concentrates the mind.
He observes with equanimity at the proper time;
that yogi is skilled in timing.
At what time should there be exertion?
At what time is there restraint?
When is it the time for praise, and of what nature is the time for tranquility?
How does it show the time for equanimity of mind to the yogin?
When the mind is sluggish, there is exertion.
One should restrain the agitated mind;
one should gladden the mind that has become disenchanted.
When the mind is uplifted,
neither sluggish nor agitated,
that is the time for serenity.
One should delight the mind within.
By this very means,
when it has become concentrated;
Knowing the mind to be concentrated,
one should maintain equanimity for that time.
Thus does the wise one, knowing the right occasion, act.
Knowing the right time and skilled in the right time,
one should, from time to time, observe the sign of the mind.
“Investigating the Dhamma rightly at the proper time”:
investigating the Dhamma rightly as “All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” and investigating the Dhamma rightly as “All conditioned phenomena are suffering.”
“Investigating the Dhamma rightly, [he understands]:
‘All phenomena are non-self’ …pe… ‘Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation’—
investigating the Dhamma rightly.”
"Being unified, he shall dispel the darkness; thus [it was said] by the Blessed One.

"Unified" (*ekodi*) means one whose mind is one-pointed, whose mind is undistracted, whose consciousness is unshaken—namely, serenity, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and right concentration;
thus he is "become unified" (*ekodibhūto*).
He would destroy, dispel, abandon, remove, eliminate, bring to an end, and cause the non-existence of darkness— that is, the darkness of lust,
the darkness of hatred, the darkness of delusion, the darkness of views, the darkness of conceit, the darkness of the defilements, and the darkness of misconduct—
which causes blindness, causes lack of vision, causes ignorance, obstructs wisdom, belongs to the side of affliction, and does not lead to Nibbāna.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence.
Furthermore, he is "Bhagavā" because his lust is destroyed; he is "Bhagavā" because his hatred is destroyed; he is "Bhagavā" because his delusion is destroyed;

he is "Bhagavā" because his conceit is destroyed; he is "Bhagavā" because his views are destroyed; he is "Bhagavā" because the thorns are destroyed; he is "Bhagavā" because the defilements are destroyed.
The Blessed One has cultivated, analyzed, and thoroughly analyzed the jewel of the Dhamma; the Blessed One brings an end to states of existence;
the Blessed One is one whose body is developed, whose virtue is developed, whose mind is developed, and whose wisdom is developed;
or else, the Blessed One frequented remote forest and woodland dwellings that were quiet, with little sound, secluded from people, and free from the bustle of men.
"Bhagavā" means "one worthy of seclusion," said the Blessed One; or "Bhagavā" means "one who possesses" robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
or "Bhagavā" means "one who possesses" the flavor of meaning, the flavor of the Dhamma, the flavor of liberation, higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom;
or "Bhagavā" means "one who possesses" the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, the four...

"Of the formless attainments," said the Blessed One; "or rather, the Blessed One is a possessor of the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive dwellings in attainment," said the Blessed One;

"or rather, the Blessed One is a possessor of the ten developments of perception, the ten kasiṇa attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, and the attainment of the foul," said the Blessed One. He is a possessor.
Or the Blessed One is “Bhagavā” because he possesses the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path;
or the Blessed One is “Bhagavā” because he possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four grounds of self-confidence.
"Of the four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the six qualities of a Buddha," said the Blessed One.
"Blessed One"— this name was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by friends and colleagues,
nor by kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities.
This is a designation realized by the Blessed Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree upon the simultaneous acquisition of omniscient knowledge, namely:
"The Blessed One"—one who has become unified, he dispels the darkness; thus he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā).
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having removed desire for these things,
a mindful bhikkhu whose mind is well-liberated,
examining the Dhamma correctly at the proper time, [attains peace].”
“Becoming one-pointed, he shall dispel the darkness.
(Thus said the Blessed One.
